title: Understanding Business Intelligence
group: Module 1: Introduction to BI & BI Tools
headings: Before Power BI: what "Business Intelligence" actually means
text: Module 1 · 1 Before Power BI: what "Business Intelligence" actually means Every tool-specific lesson on this site sits on top of one idea — turning raw operational data into decisions a business can act on. Worth naming explicitly before diving into any one tool. This page is a placeholder — full lesson content lands here as the class reaches this module. The framing below is real; the guided walkthrough, exercises, and quiz questions are still to come. The idea in one sentence Business Intelligence (BI) is the practice of collecting data a business already generates — sales, visits, support tickets, inventory — and turning it into something a human can look at and make a decision from, instead of it sitting unused in a database or spreadsheet. Kitchen analogy carries over: BI as a discipline is the whole meal — sourcing ingredients, cooking, plating, serving. Power BI (the tool this course teaches) is one kitchen you could cook that meal in; Tableau and QlikView, covered next, are other kitchens with the same job. What this page will cover 1 Data vs. information vs. insight. Why "we have a lot of data" and "we understand our business" are not the same claim. 2 The BI lifecycle. Source → store → model → analyze → visualize → decide — the same shape as the six-stage journey already taught on the Architecture page, one level more abstract. 3 Who uses BI, and for what. An operations manager watching a live dashboard is doing something different from a CFO reviewing a monthly report — same discipline, different cadence and depth. 4 Where this course focuses. Self-service BI — a business user building their own reports — as opposed to a dedicated data engineering team building pipelines nobody else touches. title: Power BI Architecture
group: Module 1: Introduction to BI & BI Tools
headings: From raw data to dashboard: the six-stage journey
Import vs. DirectQuery vs. Live Connection
text: Module 1 · 3 From raw data to dashboard: the six-stage journey Every Power BI report you will ever build — a Swiggy orders dashboard, a bank's loan-risk report, a hospital's bed-occupancy tracker — moves through the exact same six stages. Learn this once, and the whole tool stops feeling random. Data Sources Excel · SQL · Web Power Query clean · shape Data Model relationships DAX measures Visuals charts · reports Service cloud · refresh pull raw cleaned linked calculated published The same six stages carry every Power BI report — only the source and the business question change. Kitchen analogy: Data Sources are raw ingredients. Power Query is washing and chopping. The Data Model is the recipe linking ingredients together. DAX is the cooking method and measurements. Visuals are the plating. The Service is serving the finished dish to your guests. Every stage, explained ① Data Sources Where raw data physically lives before Power BI touches it — an Excel export, a company SQL Server database, or a public webpage. Nothing is clean yet. Example: A Zomato analyst's data source might be an Excel export of last month's orders. ② Power Query The cleaning layer — remove duplicates, fix spelling, split columns, handle blanks. Real data is never clean; this is where you make it usable. Example: Standardizing "bangalore", "Bangalore", "BANGALORE " into one clean value. ③ Data Model Where cleaned tables get connected through relationships — the same job as VLOOKUP in Excel, but automatic and drawn once for the whole report. Example: Linking a bank's Loans table to its Customers table by Customer ID. ④ DAX The formula language — Excel formulas' cousin, built for whole tables instead of single cells. This is how you create measures — numbers that don't already exist as a column. Example: Profit = SUM(Sales) − SUM(Cost) , recalculated instantly however you slice it. ⑤ Visuals & Reports The charts, maps, and tables you actually see — built in Report View. This is the "plating" step, turning numbers into a picture a human reads in five seconds. Example: "Top 5 restaurants by revenue" becomes a bar chart. ⑥ Dashboards & Service Desktop is where you build . The Power BI Service (cloud) is where you publish and share — a Report is multi-page and lives in Desktop; a Dashboard is a single-page pinboard that lives only in the Service. Example: Your CEO opens your published dashboard on their phone during a flight layover. Gateways & refresh A Gateway is a small piece of software that lets Power BI Service securely reach data sitting inside a private company network — like a sales database that never touches the public internet — so it can refresh automatically. Refresh is simply re-pulling the latest data so your numbers stay current: manual (click Refresh) or scheduled (e.g. every night at 6 AM). Import vs. DirectQuery vs. Live Connection Three ways Power BI can connect to data. For this whole course — and almost everything you'll do as a beginner — you'll use Import . Import DirectQuery Live Connection What happens Data is copied into Power BI's own memory Data stays at the source; queried live on every click Connects straight to an existing model built elsewhere Speed Very fast Can be slower Depends on the source model Freshness As of last Refresh Always live Always live Best for Beginners, small–medium data default choice Huge databases, real-time needs Reusing a shared company model Module 1 · Power BI Architecture Next: Connecting to Data Sources →

title: Connecting to Data Sources
group: Module 1: Introduction to BI & BI Tools
headings: Getting your data into Power BI — three ways
Import vs. DirectQuery vs. Live Connection
text: Module 1 · 4 Getting your data into Power BI — three ways Excel, a company database, or a public website — the click-path is almost identical every time: Get Data → pick a source → Navigator → Transform Data. Connecting to Excel Home → Get Data → Excel Workbook → select file → Navigator (tick sheet) → Transform Data Option What it does When to use Load Brings data in exactly as-is, no cleaning. Only when you're 100% sure the data is already clean — rare in real life. Transform Data Opens Power Query first so you can clean before it touches your report. your default click, always Combine Stacks multiple files/sheets with the same structure into one table. Your company saves one Excel file per month and you want all 12 as one table. Golden rule: Always click Transform Data , never Load, unless you've already inspected the data and know it's clean. Connecting to SQL Server A SQL Server is a very large, very organized Excel workbook that lives on a powerful shared computer instead of your laptop — it can hold billions of rows, many people can use it at once, and it's always "live." Server Name The address of the machine where the database lives, e.g. salesdb.company.com . Like a building address. Database Name The specific database on that server, e.g. SalesDB . One server can host many databases — like flats in a building. Authentication Windows Authentication (your company login, automatic) or Database Authentication (a separate username/password). Connection String Server + database + settings bundled into one line, e.g. Server=salesdb.company.com;Database=SalesDB; Import vs. DirectQuery vs. Live Connection Full comparison is on the Architecture page — the short version: use Import for this entire course and for almost everything you'll do as a beginner. Connecting to Web Data Home → Get Data → Web → paste URL → OK → Navigator → Transform Data Works on any public page with an HTML table — Wikipedia country/state data tables, government open-data portals (data.gov.in), public COVID dashboards, weather data. Power BI scans the page and lists every table it finds as Table 0 , Table 1 … — preview each one before loading to make sure you picked the right one. Real limitation: if the website changes its table layout later, the connection can break. This is a genuine trade-off of web scraping, not a bug in Power BI. title: SQL Server & AdventureWorks
group: Module 1: Introduction to BI & BI Tools
headings: A note on how this stays a static site
text: Module 1 · Extra SQL Server & AdventureWorks A closer look at connecting Power BI to a real SQL Server database, using Microsoft's AdventureWorks sample database as the running example — the same "Connecting to SQL Server" basics from earlier, applied end-to-end against a real multi-table database instead of a single Excel file. The connection walkthrough itself is still being built out as the class gets here. Downloading and installing the database, below, is ready now — the click-paths, screenshots, and sample queries for actually connecting Power BI to it will land here session by session. Where to download it AdventureWorks is Microsoft's own free sample database, published on GitHub under microsoft/sql-server-samples , inside samples/databases/adventure-works . It ships in three variants — use AdventureWorksDW , the data-warehouse version, to match every AdventureWorks example already on this site (Visualizations page, etc.): Variant What it is Use for this course? AdventureWorksDW Pre-built star schema — fact tables ( FactInternetSales , FactResellerSales ) plus dimension tables ( DimProduct , DimCustomer , DimDate , DimGeography …) Yes — this is the one AdventureWorks (OLTP) Full normalized transactional database, dozens of tables across 5 schemas Optional — an "advanced/realistic" detour once the star schema feels comfortable AdventureWorksLT "Light" — a small simplified subset Only if DW feels like too much at first github.com → microsoft/sql-server-samples → samples/databases/adventure-works → pick your SQL Server version → download the .bak file Grab the AdventureWorksDW20XX.bak file matching your SQL Server version (2016 through 2022 are all listed) — a .bak is a database backup file, the standard format SQL Server restores from directly. It's a few hundred MB; give it a minute to download. Free to use: AdventureWorks is released by Microsoft under the MIT license — safe to download, install, and reuse for classroom teaching with no licensing cost or restriction. How to install it (restore the .bak) Restoring is how you turn a downloaded backup file into a real, queryable database on your SQL Server instance. Open SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and connect to your local or class SQL Server instance In Object Explorer, right-click Databases → Restore Database… Choose Device as the source → click the … button → Add → browse to the downloaded AdventureWorksDW20XX.bak Under Files (left-hand page of the dialog), confirm the destination file paths look reasonable — SSMS usually gets this right automatically Click OK to start the restore — a few hundred MB typically takes under a minute on a normal laptop Verify it worked: expand Databases → AdventureWorksDW20XX → Tables and confirm you can see FactInternetSales and DimProduct in the list No SSMS installed? SSMS is a free download from Microsoft, Windows-only. On Mac/Linux, Azure Data Studio (also free, cross-platform) has an equivalent Restore flow under its Servers/Connections pane. No local SQL Server? SQL Server Developer Edition is free for non-production use, or run SQL Server in a Docker container — either way, restore the same .bak file once the instance is up. Common mistake: Downloading the OLTP AdventureWorks20XX.bak by accident instead of AdventureWorksDW20XX.bak — the file names are one letter apart and sit right next to each other on the releases page. Double-check the filename contains "DW" before restoring. What this module will cover 1 Getting AdventureWorks running. Restoring the sample database (or connecting to a shared class instance) so everyone is querying the same data. 2 Get Data → SQL Server, for real. Server name, database name, and authentication against an actual multi-table database instead of a single Excel file. 3 Import vs. DirectQuery, revisited. Why the choice matters more once the source is a real database that many people query at once. 4 Modeling AdventureWorks' relationships. A real star-schema-shaped set of tables — Sales, Products, Customers — instead of the single flat tables used earlier in the course. A note on how this stays a static site This page is reference material, not a live connection — GitHub Pages only serves static files, so it can't reach into a private SQL Server the way Power BI Desktop on your own machine can. What lands here is the same kind of content as the rest of the course: click-paths, screenshots, and sample queries to follow along with in your own Power BI Desktop. Large files AdventureWorks database backups and full table exports are too large for this repository. Once ready, they'll be linked from here the same way the rest of the course links to files — the only difference is where the file lives: Source Used for In this site Small CSVs, same as the practice datasets — direct download link, like the rest of the course. External · Google Drive The full AdventureWorks backup / large exports — linked out instead of committed here. Not yet published for this module. title: Navigating the Interface
group: Module 1: Introduction to BI & BI Tools
headings: Six zones. Once you can name them, you can navigate them.
text: Module 1 · 5 Six zones. Once you can name them, you can navigate them. Power BI Desktop looks intimidating for about twenty minutes. Every screen you'll ever see is built from the same six zones below — learn the map once. Home Insert Modeling View ① Ribbon Report Canvas ② your visuals live here e.g. "Sales by Category" Visualizations ③ click a chart icon to add it Fields ④ drag columns onto visuals ▸ Sales ▸ HR Filters ⑤ restrict what a visual shows ● Report ○ Data ○ Model ⑥ Page Navigation The six zones of Power BI Desktop — every screen you'll use today is a variation of this layout. Zone Purpose When you use it ① Ribbon Home · Insert · Modeling · View Home = Get Data, Refresh, Publish. Insert = logos, text, buttons. Modeling = relationships & DAX measures. Home starts every session; Modeling whenever tables need linking or a calculation is needed. ② Report Canvas The blank page where visuals are placed and arranged. Every time you design what the dashboard looks like. ③ Visualizations Pane The palette of chart types — bar, pie, line, map, and 30+ others. Anytime you want to add a new chart. ④ Fields Pane Every table and column available — your ingredient list. Constantly — you drag from here onto every chart you build. ⑤ Filters Pane Restricts what data shows, on one visual, the page, or the whole report — without deleting anything. To focus a view, e.g. "2025 only" or "exclude cancelled orders." ⑥ Page Navigation Tabs at the bottom to switch between report pages, plus the Report / Data / Model view switcher. Multi-page dashboards; switching to Data View to sanity-check a column, or Model View to check relationships. Common mix-up: Model View is only for relationships — it is not where you build charts. That's Report View. Students confuse these two constantly in week one. Module 1 · Navigating the Interface Next: Basic Visualizations →

title: Basic Visualizations
group: Module 1: Introduction to BI & BI Tools
headings: Twelve charts. One rule: every chart answers a business question.
Reference: a few more chart types
Formatting that makes it look professional
text:
Module 1 · 6 Twelve charts. One rule: every chart answers a business question. If you can't say what question a chart answers, don't build it. Basic charts first, then the building blocks, then the ones with more moving parts — click any card to see steps, formatting, best practices, and common mistakes. Terms like Axis , Legend , and Values are click-to-define wherever you see them on this site. Which chart, when? Business question Chart Avoid when… Compare a number across categories Bar Chart More than ~10–12 categories Show parts of a whole Pie Chart More than 5 categories (Rule of 5) Show change over time Line Chart Comparing unrelated categories Show one critical headline number KPI Card You need more than 4–6 things at once Show progress toward a goal Gauge Chart Comparing multiple items at once Show relationship between two numbers Scatter Plot Only one number available, 10 points Show geographic distribution Map Precise comparison matters more than location Show hierarchy + proportion together Tree Map Only one category level exists Show a running total moving through gains and losses Waterfall Chart Too many steps (8+) — bars get too thin to read Show stage-by-stage drop-off Funnel Chart Steps aren't naturally sequential/shrinking Compare two measures with different scales together Combo Chart The two measures don't share a meaningful common axis Show exact numbers across a grid, not just a picture Matrix / Table You need people to feel a pattern at a glance, not read numbers The core charts, in depth Every chart below includes an AdventureWorksDW example — deliberately built from a single table, no joins . Every field-well mapping shows the table name up front and animates the column flowing into its well, so it's obvious at a glance what's being dragged where. Full connection walkthrough: SQL Server & AdventureWorks . Column names match the standard AdventureWorksDW schema — worth a quick glance at your own restored copy before class. Reference: a few more chart types Not core to this course, but worth recognizing when you see them. Lighter treatment than the charts above — no full steps/mistakes breakdown, just what they're for and a single-table AdventureWorksDW example where a fair one exists. Formatting that makes it look professional Six habits that separate a "technically correct" chart from one people trust. Click any card for the exact clicks and a concrete before/after. Module 1 · Basic Visualizations Next: Module 1 Assignment → fieldflow chip flowline chip well margin-top:12px font-size:.85rem;font-weight:700;margin-bottom:8px pill table font-size:.83rem;color:var(--text-muted);margin-top:8px margin:14px 0 ${v.src} ${v.alt} Basic Charts Bar Chart Sales by Category Compares a number across categories, side by side — the single most useful chart in business analytics. A Flipkart category manager asking "which product category sells the most?" More than ~10–12 categories, or showing a trend over time (use a Line Chart instead). Visualizations pane → Clustered Column Chart Drag DimProduct[Color] into X-axis Drag DimProduct[ListPrice] into Y-axis (set to Average) Sort descending via the "..." menu Turn on Data Labels Sort biggest-to-smallest unless there's a natural order like months. One consistent color unless Legend is used meaningfully. Leaving the default ugly auto-title ("Sum of Sales by Category"). Using a Bar Chart for a trend over time. Look at the tallest bar first — that's your headline. The shortest is often the more interesting question. DimProduct DimProduct[Color] Axis (X) DimProduct[ListPrice] (Average) Values (Y) DimProduct[Weight] Tooltip Color, List Price, and Weight all live directly on DimProduct — single table, no join. The Tooltip well adds Weight as extra on-hover detail without changing what the bars themselves show. Basic Charts Pie Chart Market Share by Category Shows how a whole is divided into parts — each slice as a percentage of the total. A telecom company showing market share by brand in one glance. More than 5 categories (the Rule of 5), comparing exact values precisely, or trends over time. Visualizations pane → Pie Chart Drag DimProduct[Class] into Legend Drag DimProduct[ProductKey] into Values (set to Count) Data labels → Category, Percent of total Maximum 5 slices. Always show percentage, not just raw numbers. Using pie charts for 8+ categories — a "rainbow wheel" nobody can read. Forgetting percentage labels. A pie chart answers exactly one question: what's the biggest piece of the pie? Nothing else. DimProduct DimProduct[Class] Legend DimProduct[ProductKey] (Count) Values Class only has three values (L / M / H), so it respects the Rule of 5 automatically. Some products may have a blank Class — worth a quick Power Query check before presenting. Basic Charts Line Chart Monthly Sales Trend Shows how a number changes over time — the only chart built specifically for trend. A Swiggy ops team tracking daily order volume to spot growth, dips, or a viral spike. Comparing unrelated categories (use Bar), or showing a single point in time (use a Card). Visualizations pane → Line Chart Drag FactInternetSales[OrderDate] into X-axis Drag FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] into Y-axis (set to Sum) Drill to Month for a cleaner view Analytics pane → add a Trend line Always sort the X-axis chronologically — needs a real Date type, not text. Limit to 1–3 lines max. A Date column still typed as Text sorts alphabetically, not chronologically, producing a nonsensical zig-zag. Look at direction and bumps, not just height. A sawtooth pattern usually means a weekly cycle. An annotated line chart showing three things at once: an overall upward trend shown as a dashed reference line, a regular up-down seasonality cycle in the data itself, and one sharp one-off spike near the end of the series, called out for investigation before presenting. Three things live in every trend line at once — learn to separate them before you say anything about "the trend." FactInternetSales FactInternetSales[OrderDate] (by Month) Axis (X) FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] (Sum) Values (Y) FactInternetSales carries its own OrderDate column — Power BI builds a Year/Quarter/Month hierarchy straight from it, no separate date table required. Building Blocks KPI Card Total Sales, Profit, Orders, AOV Displays one single, critical number as large as possible — the headline number of your dashboard. The four numbers a Zomato regional head checks first every morning. More than 4–6 cards on one page — beyond that, nothing feels important anymore. Visualizations pane → Card Drag FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] into Fields (set to Sum) for Total Sales For Total Orders, drag FactInternetSales[SalesOrderNumber] into Fields and change aggregation to Count (Distinct) For Average Order Value, write a DAX measure using DIVIDE Round large numbers (Format → Display units). Keep the label short — "Total Sales," not a full sentence. A KPI with no context, or using Sum when Average was intended. KPI cards are read in under 2 seconds — if someone has to think about what it means, it failed. FactInternetSales FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] (Sum) Total Sales FactInternetSales[SalesOrderNumber] (Distinct Count) Total Orders Profit and AOV are measures, not raw columns: Profit = SUM(SalesAmount) − SUM(TotalProductCost); AOV = DIVIDE(SUM(SalesAmount), DISTINCTCOUNT(SalesOrderNumber)). Both source columns are native to FactInternetSales — still one table. Building Blocks Gauge Chart Monthly Target vs Actual Shows progress of a single number toward a goal — like a car's speedometer. A bank branch manager tracking "have we hit this month's loan disbursement target?" Comparing multiple items — a gauge shows exactly ONE value against ONE target. Visualizations pane → Gauge Drag FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] into Value (set to Sum, the Actual/needle) Set Minimum (usually 0) Set Maximum (~120–150% of target) Set Target value in the Format pane Only use for a single, high-importance goal metric. Keep Maximum realistic. Forgetting to set a Target — it becomes just a fancier, less clear KPI Card. Only 3 readings matter: behind goal, on track, or exceeded. If you need more nuance, pick a different chart. FactInternetSales FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] (Sum), filtered to this month Value typed manually in the Format pane Target The month filter comes from FactInternetSales' own OrderDate column — still no join needed. AdventureWorksDW has no built-in "target" column, same as the generic lesson. Advanced Charts Scatter Plot Sales vs Profit Shows the relationship between two numeric measures at once — reveals whether they move together (positive correlation), move oppositely (negative correlation), or show no real pattern at all. Also the fastest way to spot clusters and outliers that a bar or line chart would hide. Do higher-cost products also carry higher list prices, or are some best-sellers actually thin-margin traps? Every dot above the diagonal 1:1 line is priced above cost — the higher above the line, the fatter the margin. Only one number to show, fewer than ~10 data points, or when the two measures use wildly different scales/units without a secondary axis. Visualizations pane → Scatter Chart Drag DimProduct[StandardCost] into X-axis Drag DimProduct[ListPrice] into Y-axis Drag DimProduct[ProductLine] into Legend Drag DimProduct[Class] into Small multiples Always label both axes clearly with real units. Add a trend line (Analytics pane → Trend line) when the direction of the relationship needs to be called out, not just implied. Use color/Legend to split by a category only when that category is the actual point of the analysis, not for decoration. Plotting two measures with no logical relationship. Ignoring outliers instead of investigating them — a lonely dot is often a data-entry error, but sometimes it's the most important row in the table. And remember: correlation is not causation, and a tidy-looking cloud can still hide a non-linear relationship. Read the shape of the whole cloud before any single dot: tight and diagonal means strong correlation, wide and round means weak or none. In the AdventureWorksDW example, the diagonal is a 1:1 reference line — every dot above it is priced above its cost, and the vertical gap between a dot and the line is that product's markup. The lonely dot far from the cluster is either a data error or a genuinely unusual product worth a closer look. Left: a scatter plot of DimProduct StandardCost versus ListPrice, dots colored by Product Line — Road, Mountain, Standard — with a dashed 1:1 reference line and one outlier circled far above the cluster. Right: the same data split into three small-multiple scatter plots, one per Class — L, M, H — with the cluster shifting up and to the right as Class increases. Cost vs. price for every product — markup is the vertical gap above the 1:1 line. Split by Class on the right shows why small multiples exist: three clean stories instead of one crowded chart. DimProduct DimProduct[StandardCost] Axis (X) DimProduct[ListPrice] Axis (Y) DimProduct[ProductLine] Legend DimProduct[Class] Small multiples Cost and price live on the same table, so this reads as pure markup per product — the gap between a dot and a 1:1 line is margin. ProductLine on AdventureWorksDW uses short codes — R (Road), M (Mountain), S (Standard), T (Touring) — worth spelling out in the Legend's data labels so the audience isn't left guessing. Small multiples by Class splits one crowded scatter into three side-by-side mini-scatters (Low/Medium/High), one table, no join. Advanced Charts Sales by State Shows geographic distribution of a number — instantly answers "where" questions. A Blinkit ops head asking "which cities should we open more dark stores in?" When precise value comparison matters more than location, or fewer than ~4–5 locations. Visualizations pane → Filled Map (or Map for bubbles) Drag DimGeography[StateProvinceName] into Location Drag DimGeography[GeographyKey] into Color saturation (Filled, set to Count) or Size (Bubble) Pair a map with a bar chart of the same data — map for "where," bar for "how much exactly." Relying on a map as the ONLY way to show regional performance — circle/shade size is hard to compare precisely. Two more traps worth knowing by name: bubble maps that scale by radius instead of area exaggerate differences, and place names that exist in more than one country/state can geocode to the wrong spot entirely. Use to show WHERE something is happening; use a bar chart to know precisely HOW MUCH more one place has. Left: bubble-size distortion — doubling a bubble's radius for a 2x value makes its area look 4x bigger, misleading; scaling by area instead correctly shows a 2x-looking difference. Right: ambiguous place names — a pin labeled Georgia could mean the US state or the country, and geocoding has to guess without more context. Two ways a map quietly lies even when the data behind it is correct — a distorted bubble scale, and a geocoder guessing wrong on an ambiguous name. DimGeography DimGeography[StateProvinceName] Location DimGeography[GeographyKey] (Count) Values This counts cities on file per state, not sales — geography is a dimension-only table by design, so a real sales-by-state map needs a join through DimCustomer to FactInternetSales. This single-table version is the honest stand-in until joins are covered. Advanced Charts Tree Map Revenue by Category & Sub-Category Shows part-to-whole AND hierarchy at the same time, using nested rectangles sized by value. An Amazon category head viewing Revenue by Category, then Sub-Category, in one single view. When exact value comparison matters, or you only have one level of category. Visualizations pane → Treemap Drag DimProduct[Class] into the Category well Drag DimProduct[Style] into the same well, below it Drag DimProduct[ProductKey] into Values (set to Count) Limit to 2 hierarchy levels. Use only when hierarchy AND proportion both matter. Using a Tree Map when a simple bar chart would communicate faster and more precisely. Scan for the biggest rectangle first, then look inside it — what's carrying that category? title: Custom Visuals
headings: Thirty built-in charts cover most questions. Custom visuals are for the ones that don't.
What a custom visual actually is
When to reach for one — and when to stay native
Is it safe to use? Evaluating trustworthiness
Performance: test before it ships company-wide
Find, vet, and justify one custom visual
text: Module 2 · Custom Visuals Thirty built-in charts cover most questions. Custom visuals are for the ones that don't. AppSource is Power BI's plug-in marketplace — hundreds of extra custom visuals beyond the ~30 built-in chart types covered on the Visualizations page, built by Microsoft, its partners, and independent developers. They drop into the same Visualizations pane and read fields exactly the way a built-in chart does — but every one you add runs third-party code inside your report, so knowing when to reach for one, and how to check it first, matters as much as knowing it exists. The path every custom visual takes, from the marketplace to your canvas. What a custom visual actually is Once installed, a custom visual behaves exactly like Bar Chart or Line Chart — drag a field into a well, format it in the same pane, save it with the rest of the report. The only difference is where it came from: Microsoft AppSource, or occasionally a file, instead of the box. Some are published by Microsoft itself, some by analytics consulting firms, many by independent developers — anyone can publish one, which is exactly why the trust-check later on this page matters. A handful of categories show up again and again in real business reporting: Business question Custom visual category Why a built-in chart falls short Which words come up most in open-text feedback? Word Cloud No built-in visual sizes text by frequency Show overlapping tasks, stays, or projects on a real date timeline Gantt Chart Bar charts can't position a bar between two actual dates Show how volume splits and flows between stages or groups Sankey / Chord Diagram No built-in visual draws flow width between nodes Compare a value against a target and performance bands, densely Bullet Chart A Gauge fits one metric per screen; Bullet fits many in a row Compare several dimensions of one item at once (a scorecard) Radar / Spider Chart No built-in visual plots multiple axes around a center point Show daily activity across many months (attendance, logins) Calendar Heatmap A Matrix holds the numbers but can't shade like a calendar grid None of these are required anywhere else in this course — they're here because you will eventually meet a business question a built-in chart genuinely cannot answer, and you should know where to look. When to reach for one — and when to stay native Reach for a custom visual Stay with a built-in visual The question A built-in chart structurally cannot show it — e.g. real date-range bars, word frequency, flow between groups A bar, line, map, KPI card, or table would answer it just as well Speed Worth testing and timing before it ships Microsoft-optimized, fastest by default default choice Support You've confirmed the publisher is active and the visual was updated recently No dependency on a third party ever going quiet Risk You've vetted it (see below) and it's going into a low-stakes report first No extra security or performance review needed Default bias: start every report with built-in visuals. Reach into AppSource only when you can name the specific business question a built-in chart cannot answer — never because a custom visual "looks more advanced." Advantages and disadvantages, stated plainly Advantages ✓ Answers questions built-in charts structurally can't — real date-range bars, word frequency, flow between groups ✓ Same drag-and-drop field wells as any built-in chart — no new mental model once it's installed ✓ Most are free, and several — including many of Microsoft's own — are Certified and actively maintained Disadvantages ✕ Third-party code runs inside your report — a real security surface, larger for uncertified visuals ✕ Can render slower than native visuals, especially on large tables (see Performance, below) ✕ An organization's Power BI admin can restrict which custom visuals are allowed tenant-wide — a report that works on your laptop can fail to render for a colleague ✕ No continuity guarantee — a publisher can stop updating a visual, or pull it from AppSource, with no Microsoft backstop the way the built-in ~30 have Finding a custom visual Visualizations pane → "..." More options → Get more visuals → search or browse a category → Add The same catalog is also a standalone website — AppSource (appsource.microsoft.com) — worth browsing outside Desktop while you're still planning a report. It's easier to compare several visuals side by side, read full descriptions, and check ratings there than inside the narrow pane. Anything found on the website gets added to a report the same way, from inside Desktop. Importing one into your report From AppSource, inside Desktop Visualizations pane → "..." → Get more visuals Search by name, or browse a category Open the listing — check publisher, rating, and the Certified badge before adding (next section) Add — the icon appears at the bottom of the Visualizations pane, ready to use like any built-in chart From a downloaded .pbiviz file Visualizations pane → "..." → Import a visual from a file Browse to the .pbiviz file — common for an internal company-built visual, or one shared outside AppSource entirely Confirm the security prompt — Power BI always warns that a visual from outside AppSource hasn't been through Microsoft's review The visual appears in the Visualizations pane for that report only Treat a .pbiviz file like any unfamiliar executable: it's a packaged bundle of code, not a picture. Only import one from a source — a colleague, your IT team, a known vendor — you'd trust with access to whatever data you drop into it. Is it safe to use? Evaluating trustworthiness Signal What to check Why it matters Certified badge A checkmark shown right on the AppSource listing Means Microsoft reviewed it for security and performance — the closest thing to an official stamp Publisher Microsoft, a known analytics partner, or an unnamed individual account An accountable, actively-maintained publisher is lower long-term risk Ratings & review count Star rating, and how many organizations actually left one A handful of reviews tells you far less than hundreds Data access requested Whether it only renders the fields you give it, or calls out to an external service (a mapping or AI API, say) Sending company data outside Power BI is a real governance question, not a technicality Open source Whether the code is publicly published — many, including several of Microsoft's own, are on GitHub You or your IT team can inspect what it actually does instead of taking the listing's word for it Certified isn't the same as risk-free — it means Microsoft confirmed a baseline. For a report built on this course's HR, Banking, or Hospital data, treat "uncertified + unknown publisher + almost no reviews" as a hard no, not a maybe. Licensing, in general terms Free No cost to add or use. Most custom visuals on AppSource fall here, including many of Microsoft's own. Freemium Free to add, with a paid tier unlocking extra formatting, export options, or higher data-point limits. Paid / subscription Requires a license key, sign-in, or subscription from the publisher before it renders at all — terms set entirely by them, not Microsoft. Licensing lives with the publisher, not Power BI. Before building a report around a paid visual, check the listing's pricing page and confirm whether the license covers just you, or everyone who'll open the published report — that per-user vs. per-report line varies by publisher and is worth confirming in writing, not assuming. Performance: test before it ships company-wide Native (built-in) visual Custom visual Render speed Optimized by Microsoft, fastest by default Varies by publisher — can be noticeably slower, especially uncertified ones Large datasets Built and tested at enterprise scale Not guaranteed — test explicitly on a full-size table, not just a 100-row practice file Support Microsoft, as part of the product, indefinitely Whoever published it — can pause updates or stop entirely A visual that feels instant on your laptop with a small sample can lag badly once it's facing the real row count in production. Add it to a copy of the report, test with realistic data volumes, and time it — before it ships in a report the whole company opens every Monday morning. Guided walkthrough Gantt Chart — Hospital dataset: patient length of stay Concept: A Gantt Chart visual draws one horizontal bar per row, positioned and sized by a start date and an end date — something no built-in Power BI chart does. The closest built-in option, a stacked bar chart, has no way to place a bar between two real calendar dates. Business question: A hospital ops manager wants to see, at a glance, which patients are occupying a bed far longer than others in the same department — a length-of-stay outlier is either a genuinely complex case or a discharge-process bottleneck worth a follow-up question. Field mapping Table: Hospital Hospital[Patient] Category (task) Hospital[Admission Date] Start Date Hospital[Discharge Date] End Date Hospital[Department] Legend All four fields live on the one Hospital table — no join needed to build this. Steps Download Hospital_Clean.csv from the Datasets page → Get Data → Text/CSV → Transform Data In Power Query, confirm Admission Date and Discharge Date are typed as Date, not Text — a Gantt visual can't place a text value on a date axis Visualizations pane → "..." → Get more visuals → search "Gantt" → check the listing, then Add Build the field mapping above: Patient into the task well, Admission Date into Start, Discharge Date into End, Department into Legend Optional: add a calculated column in DAX so bars can be sorted or labeled by duration directly: Length of Stay = Hospital[Discharge Date] − Hospital[Admission Date] Format → sort by Start Date so the timeline reads left to right in admission order, and turn on data labels for the duration Once built, a pattern like this is what you're looking for — illustrative values, not the real file's numbers: Patient · Cardiology 4 days typical Patient · Cardiology 11 days above dept. average Patient · Maternity 2 days typical Best practice: Keep Department in the Legend well — length of stay only makes sense compared within the same specialty, since a normal Maternity stay and a normal Cardiology stay are very different numbers. Common mistake: Building the visual before checking the two date columns actually parsed as Date — the same trap as a Line Chart X-axis, except here it can silently misdraw every bar's length, not just the sort order. Try it yourself: Swap Department for Doctor in the Legend well — does the same length-of-stay pattern hold per doctor, or only per department? Exercise Practice · Custom Visuals Find, vet, and justify one custom visual 1 Pick any dataset already used in this course (Sales, HR, Retail, Banking, or Hospital) and name one real business question a built-in chart genuinely cannot answer. 2 Search AppSource for a custom visual that answers it, and note its Certified status, publisher, and review count. 3 Import it and build it against your chosen dataset. 4 Write two sentences: why a built-in chart couldn't do this job, and what you checked before trusting the visual. title: Groups & Histograms
headings: One combines categories. The other bins a number. Both exist to stop a chart from drowning in detail.
Groups: turning too many categories into a few that matter
Histograms: seeing the shape of one number
text: Module 2 · Groups & Histograms One combines categories. The other bins a number. Both exist to stop a chart from drowning in detail. Two small features, taught together because they solve the same underlying problem from opposite directions. A group takes a column that already has categories — City, Diagnosis, Department — and collapses too many of them into a few that actually mean something on a chart. Binning does the reverse: it takes a column that has NO categories at all, just a continuous number, and manufactures ranges out of it so it can be charted like one. Neither one changes a single row of source data — both just change what the chart is allowed to look like. Groups: turning too many categories into a few that matter Same underlying rows, before and after grouping — fewer, more readable bars. What grouping is, and why it's worth doing Concept: A group combines several existing values of a category field into one broader bucket — a new field, sitting alongside the original, that a chart can use instead. The original column is untouched; Power Query never runs, nothing in the source file changes. Why it matters: Some category columns are genuinely too fine-grained for a summary view. A retail chain with stores in 15 cities produces a Bar Chart with 15 thin bars — technically correct, practically unreadable. Grouped down to 4 regions, the same data becomes a chart an executive can read in two seconds. Real-world example: A Zomato ops lead doesn't plan city-by-city in a board meeting — they plan by region. The underlying orders still happened in specific cities; the chart just needs to speak at region level. Grouping is not the same as fixing dirty data. If "Bengaluru" and "Banglore" show up as two different values because of a typo, that's a Power Query cleanup (Replace Values), not a group. Group AFTER the category values are already clean and consistent — grouping 15 correctly-spelled cities into 4 regions is a completely different job from fixing a 16th city that's really a misspelling of one of the other 15. How grouping works mechanically — two ways in Power BI offers the same feature from two different starting points — pick whichever one you're already looking at. From a visual Build a Bar Chart with the category field on the Axis In the chart, Ctrl-click to select several bars/values at once Right-click the selection → Group Rename the new group, then repeat for the next set of values From the Fields pane Right-click the field in the Fields pane New group Move values into named groups in the dialog, or leave ungrouped values as "Other" OK — a new field appears, e.g. "City (groups)" Best practice: Give every group a real business name (Region, Age Band, Diagnosis Category) — the default "City (groups)" is fine as a technical field name, but the individual bucket labels inside it should read like something a manager would actually say out loud. Common mistake: Leaving several values dumped into an unlabeled "Other" bucket that ends up larger than any real group — if "Other" is the tallest bar, the grouping logic needs a second pass. Before/After — Retail dataset: 15 cities → 4 regions Business question: A Retail chain manager wants Sales by location for a leadership deck — not 15 city bars nobody outside operations recognizes, but 4 regions everyone in the room already thinks in. Field mapping Table: Retail Retail[City] right-click values in the chart → Group new field: City (groups) Axis (X) Retail[Sales] (Sum) Values (Y) Before — Retail[City] (15 values) After — City (groups) Mumbai, Pune, Nagpur, Nashik West Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Coimbatore South Delhi, Jaipur, Lucknow, Chandigarh North Kolkata, Patna, Bhubaneswar East Retail[City] and Retail[Sales] both live on the one Retail table — no join needed. Download Retail_Clean.csv from the Datasets page to follow along. Step-by-step workflow Load Retail_Clean.csv and build a Bar Chart: Retail[City] into Axis, Sum of Sales into Values — this is the "before," 15 thin bars Ctrl-click the bars for Mumbai, Pune, Nagpur, Nashik Right-click the selection → Group → name it "West" Repeat for South, North, and East Rename the new field from "City (groups)" to "Region" in the Fields pane for a cleaner axis title Swap Axis from Retail[City] to the new Region field — 15 bars become 4 Try it yourself: Build the same grouping on the Hospital dataset instead — collapse the many individual values in Hospital[Diagnosis] into a handful of broader categories (say, Cardiac, Respiratory, Orthopedic, Other) and compare a Bill Amount summary before and after. Groups don't disappear when you undo them. Because the original column is never touched, deleting a group field or unchecking a value from it is completely safe — the source data was never at risk in the first place. Histograms: seeing the shape of one number What a histogram actually shows Concept: A histogram shows the distribution of ONE numeric field — how many rows fall into each of several equal-width ranges across the full spread of values, from lowest to highest. Why it matters: An average hides everything interesting. "Average loan amount: ₹4.2 lakh" doesn't tell you whether most borrowers cluster tightly around that number, or whether a few huge loans are dragging the average up while most people borrow far less. Real-world example: A bank's credit team doesn't just want the average loan size — they want to know whether most loans are small and a handful are huge (which changes how risk should be priced), or whether loan sizes cluster tightly around a typical amount (which means one pricing rule fits most customers). Histogram vs. Bar Chart — the mix-up everyone makes once Both look like a row of vertical bars, which is exactly why they get confused. The difference isn't how they look — it's where the x-axis comes from. Bar Chart Histogram X-axis An existing category already in the data (City, Product, Department) Manufactured by binning — a continuous number sliced into equal-width ranges that don't exist as values in the source data One bar = One real category value One numeric range (a "bin"), e.g. ₹2–4 lakh Bar order Any order you choose — often sorted by size Fixed — must run low to high, since it's a number line Bar spacing Gaps between bars — categories are separate, unrelated things Bars touch, no gaps — the ranges are continuous and adjacent Answers "How does X compare across categories?" "How are the values of X spread out?" Common mistake: Calling a Bar Chart of "Sales by Category" a histogram because it's made of bars. If the thing on the x-axis is a name someone typed into a spreadsheet, it's a Bar Chart. If the x-axis is a range of numbers nobody typed anywhere — Power BI built it by slicing a continuous number — it's a histogram. Bins and bin size — the choice that changes the story Concept: A bin is one of the equal-width ranges a histogram slices the number line into — set either by a fixed bin size (e.g. every ₹1 lakh) or a target number of bins that Power BI divides the full range into evenly. Same underlying numbers, very different chart depending on the choice. Too few bins and every interesting bump gets smoothed into one fat, boring bar. Too many bins and small sampling gaps in the data start looking like real dips and spikes — noise dressed up as a pattern. There's rarely one mathematically "correct" bin count; there's a bin count that shows the shape honestly and one that doesn't. Try it below — same underlying loan amounts, three different bin counts: 3 bins 8 bins 20 bins When to reach for a histogram Business question Reach for "What's the average order value?" A KPI Card — one number is exactly what's asked "How are order values distributed — are most orders small with a few huge ones, or fairly consistent?" Histogram — the question is about spread, not a single figure "Are our employees' salaries clustered together or spread wide, and are there any unusual outliers?" Histogram on HR[Salary] "Which department has the highest average salary?" A Bar Chart — that's a category comparison, not a distribution question The tell: if the business question has the word "average," "typical," "distributed," "spread," or "outlier" in it, a single KPI card is probably hiding the real answer — a histogram shows what the average is quietly averaging over. Building a histogram in Power BI — and how it connects back to Groups The connection: Power BI's "New group" dialog — the same one used for cities → regions above — also works on numeric fields, with a Bin option instead of manual buckets. Numeric binning IS grouping; it's just Power BI grouping automatically by equal-width range instead of by hand-picked category. Classic approach — bin a field, then Bar Chart Right-click Banking[Loan Amount] in the Fields pane New group Group type: Bin · set Bin size (e.g. 100000) or Number of bins OK — a new field appears, e.g. "Loan Amount (bins)" Build a Clustered Column Chart: the binned field into Axis, Count of records into Values Certified Histogram Chart (AppSource) Visualizations pane → "..." → Get more visuals Search "Histogram Chart" (Microsoft-published, Certified) — see Custom Visuals for how to vet one Drag the raw Banking[Loan Amount] straight into Values — no manual binning first Use the Format pane's bin controls to change bin count live and watch the shape change Best practice: The classic bin-column approach is worth learning first — it's the same "New group" mechanic from the Groups section, so nothing new to remember. Reach for the certified visual once bin size needs to be tweaked live and re-tweaked, not once and done. Reading the shape — Banking dataset: Loan Amount Business question: A bank credit team asks — are our loans mostly one typical size, or is there a mix worth pricing differently? Field mapping Table: Banking Banking[Loan Amount] New group → Bin Loan Amount (bins) Axis (X) Banking[Customer] (Count) Values (Y) Both fields live on the one Banking table — no join needed. Download Banking_Clean.csv from the Datasets page to build this yourself; treat the shape below as illustrative, not the real file's exact numbers. Three shapes come up again and again — read in plain business language, not statistics-class language: Bell-shaped Most loans cluster around one typical size, tapering evenly on both sides. There's a genuine "normal" customer — one pricing rule reasonably fits most of them. Skewed A long tail on one side — most loans are modest, but a handful of very large ones stretch the tail right. The average sits higher than what a typical borrower actually takes. Bimodal (two peaks) Two separate humps instead of one — often means two different customer segments are mixed into one column, like small personal loans and large home loans counted together. How this changes a decision: If Loan Amount turns out right-skewed, quoting "the average loan is ₹4.2 lakh" to a planning meeting is misleading — most customers borrow well below that, and a few large loans are pulling the average up. A histogram is the chart that catches this before a wrong assumption ships into a strategy deck. Try it yourself: Build the same histogram on Banking[Credit Score] instead. A bimodal shape there — one cluster of strong scores, one cluster of weak ones, few people in between — would mean very different things for how the bank should segment its risk pricing. Exercises Exercise 1 · Groups HR dataset — Location into Region Group HR[Location] into 3–4 named regions the way Retail[City] was grouped into 4 regions above, then build a Bar Chart of Average Salary by your new Region field. Exercise 2 · Histograms Sales dataset — is Discount skewed? Bin Sales[Discount] into 8 bins and build a histogram. Is the shape bell, skewed, or bimodal — and what would that mean for how discounts are actually being applied? Module 2 · Groups & Histograms Next: Best Practices → Too few bins: the shape is gone. All this says is "most loans are somewhere in the middle" — the interesting detail is smoothed away. A reasonable bin count: a clear peak and a taper are both visible without noise drowning out the signal. Too many bins: small sampling gaps start looking like real dips and spikes. title: Visualization Best Practices
headings: The chart is right. Now make it honest, clean, and readable in three seconds.
Matching visual complexity to the audience
text: Module 2 · Best Practices The chart is right. Now make it honest, clean, and readable in three seconds. Picking the correct chart type is half the job — the Visualizations page's "Which chart, when?" table already covers that. This page is the other half: the cross-cutting formatting and design discipline that decides whether a technically-correct chart tells the truth clearly, or quietly misleads, clutters, or gets ignored. Every rule here applies no matter which of the twelve chart types you picked. Choosing the chart itself — business question → chart type, plus per-chart best practices and common mistakes — lives on the Visualizations page's "Which chart, when?" table. This page assumes the chart type is already decided and focuses only on how it's formatted and presented. Avoiding misleading charts A chart can use the "right" type and still lie. None of the tricks below require bad intent — they're often just Power BI's defaults left un-fixed — but the effect on a reader is the same either way: a false impression of how big a difference really is. Trick What it does Fix Truncated / non-zero Y-axis Starting the axis at 90 instead of 0 turns a 4% difference into what looks like a 400% difference Format pane → Y-axis → Range → set Minimum to 0, unless there's a genuinely documented reason not to Inconsistent scales between compared charts Two bar charts placed side by side, one axis maxing at 100 and the other at 1,000 — bars look similar height but represent wildly different values Lock both visuals to the same axis Minimum/Maximum in the Format pane before placing them side by side Cherry-picked date range Zooming into the three months that support the story and quietly dropping the ones that don't Default every trend to the full available history; let a viewer narrow the range themselves with a slicer, don't narrow it for them Dual axes implying false correlation Two unrelated measures plotted on independent left/right axes can be dragged into looking like they move together, when the scales were just picked to make the lines cross Only combine two measures on dual axes when they share a real, meaningful relationship — and say so in the title Same underlying numbers, two very different impressions — this is the single most common way a Power BI report misleads without anyone intending to: Needs improvement · axis starts at 80 Region C looks nearly 3× Region A — but the axis is truncated, so the visual gap is exaggerated far past the real difference. exaggerates the gap Good · zero-based axis Same three regions, same underlying numbers, axis starts at 0 — Region C is ahead, but honestly by a modest margin, not a landslide. reads honestly Common mistake: Power BI's default axis is usually zero-based, but "Auto" range on some visuals will truncate automatically once values cluster in a narrow band. Always check the Format pane's Range setting explicitly — don't assume the default protected you. Appropriate use of color Color is the fastest channel a viewer's eye reads — which is exactly why it needs the most discipline. Used well, it points straight at what matters. Used as decoration, it competes with the data for attention and usually wins. Do ✓ Pick one consistent palette for the whole report (Format pane → Theme) and stop touching it per-visual ✓ Let color mean something — the same category is always the same color across every page ✓ Choose a colorblind-safe palette (avoid pure red/green as the only distinguishing pair — roughly 1 in 12 men has some form of red-green color blindness) ✓ Use color sparingly, to highlight — one accent color on the bar that matters, neutral gray everywhere else Don't ✕ Give every category its own rainbow color just because the Legend well auto-generates one ✕ Let a category's color drift between pages — Electronics blue on page 1, Electronics green on page 3 ✕ Rely on red vs. green alone to signal good vs. bad — pair it with an icon, label, or shape too ✕ Color a chart just because a blank white bar "looks unfinished" — color without meaning is noise The same five categories, formatted two ways: Needs improvement · color as decoration A different color per bar for no reason — the eye tries to find meaning in the color choice and finds none. competes with the data Good · one accent, used to highlight Neutral teal for every bar, one accent color on the single bar that's the point of the chart — the eye lands there first. points at the insight Consistent formatting across a report A report that switches fonts, number formats, or color schemes between pages reads as unfinished even when every number on it is correct — inconsistency is itself a signal that erodes trust before anyone checks the data. One theme View → Themes → pick or build one custom theme, apply it once, and stop hand-picking colors per visual afterward. One font Set it in the theme, not visual-by-visual — a report mixing Segoe UI titles with Calibri axis labels looks assembled from spare parts. One number format Decide once whether currency is ₹, $, or unlabeled, how many decimal places, and apply that same rule to every measure on every page. Titles and labels Power BI's auto-generated title — "Sum of Sales by Category" — describes the mechanics of the chart, not what it tells you. A real title does the reader's first thinking step for them. Needs improvement "Sum of SalesAmount by Region" Restates the field names. Says nothing a viewer couldn't already see in the Fields pane. Good "West leads every other region by 2×" States the finding directly. A viewer who reads only the title still walks away informed. Axis and legend labels deserve the same attention: rename a field-derived label like "SUM(Sales_Amt)" to plain "Sales ($)" in the Format pane before a report ever leaves your laptop. Data labels A data label prints the exact number directly on the chart — genuinely useful when there are few enough data points to read cleanly, actively harmful once there are too many. Chart is… Data labels Why A KPI Card, Gauge, or a Bar Chart with ≤ 8–10 bars turn on Few enough points that the exact number adds precision without crowding A dense Line Chart (daily data across a year) or a Scatter Plot with 100+ points leave off Labels overlap into an unreadable smear — let the shape of the line or cluster carry the message, use a tooltip for exact values on hover A Pie Chart on, as % of total A pie only works if the reader can see the actual share each slice represents, not just relative size Number formatting ✓ Display units: Format pane → Display units → Thousands/Millions turns "1,240,000" into a much faster-to-read "1.24M" ✓ Consistent decimal places: pick one rule (e.g. currency to 0 decimals, percentages to 1) and apply it to every measure of that type, everywhere in the report ✓ Currency symbols: set once in the measure's format string, not retyped as text in a title — a hardcoded "$" breaks the moment the report is reused for a different currency Sorting Bars sorted biggest-to-smallest let a reader find the winner and the laggard in one glance, without hunting across the chart. That's the default for anything without an inherent order. The one exception: when categories have a natural order of their own — months of the year, days of the week, a funnel's stages — keep that natural order instead of re-sorting by value. Forcing "Jan, Jun, Mar, Dec…" into value order destroys the thing a time axis is supposed to communicate. Reducing clutter Every gridline, border, and legend a Power BI default turns on is a small tax on the reader's attention. If it isn't earning its place, it's competing with the data that is. Element Usually Keep it when… Gridlines Turn off or lighten (Format pane → Gridlines) The chart genuinely needs precise value reading, not just shape comparison Visual border Turn off — let a card's background do the separating Rarely — borders mostly just add visual weight Legend Turn off when there's only one series, or when data labels already name each bar Multiple series/colors that genuinely need a key to decode Axis title Often removable if the chart title already makes the axis obvious The unit isn't otherwise clear from the chart title or labels Common mistake: Formatting a chart once and never revisiting it. After data labels, a title, and units are all on, go back and turn off anything that no longer earns its place — most reports get cluttered by addition, never by a single bad decision. Accessibility ✓ Contrast: text and important marks should be clearly readable against their background — Power BI's built-in themes are checked for this; a fully custom palette should be too ✓ Never color alone: pair red/green status with an icon, label, or pattern, so the meaning still lands for a colorblind viewer or a black-and-white printout ✓ Alt text: Format pane → General → Alt text — a short description of what the visual shows, read aloud by screen readers Mobile and responsive considerations A report built and tested only on a wide desktop monitor can be genuinely unusable on the phone where a manager actually opens it between meetings. View → Phone layout → drag visuals into a single-column stack → reorder so the most critical visual is at the top Power BI keeps a separate phone layout from the desktop one — building it isn't automatic. The KPI or single chart someone needs first (this month's headline number, say) belongs at the very top of that stack; everything a viewer might scroll past should be exploratory detail, not the answer to the question they opened the report to ask. Avoiding unnecessary 3D effects 3D is flatly worse for reading data accurately — a 3D pie or column chart distorts the visual size of the slice or bar closest to the "camera," making it look larger than its actual value while the far side looks smaller. There is no business scenario on this course's data where a 3D effect adds real information; it only adds a perception error. Stick to flat 2D charts. Highlighting important insights A dashboard that presents forty numbers with equal visual weight makes the reader do the work of finding the one that matters. Do that work for them. A callout box A text box or the built-in Report Page Tooltip pattern that states the one-sentence takeaway in plain language, placed near the chart it explains — not buried in a title. Conditional highlight color One bar (or one row, via conditional formatting ) in the accent color while the rest stay neutral — the same technique used in the color mockup above. Keeping dashboards focused A page built to answer "how did we do this quarter" and a page built to answer "which customers are at risk of churning" are two different pages, even if they'd both technically fit on one. One clear purpose per page beats a single page trying to be everything the company owns data about. Common mistake: "Let's just add it to the main dashboard" as the default answer to every new stakeholder request. A page that tries to answer every question ends up answering none of them clearly — a focused page a viewer understands in ten seconds is worth more than a comprehensive one they give up on. Matching visual complexity to the audience Audience Wants Report shape An executive Three numbers and a trend, in under 10 seconds A handful of KPI cards plus one trend line — headline page first, everything else behind a click An analyst The full table, ability to slice and drill A Matrix/Table with slicers, drill-down enabled, and a Tooltip well carrying extra detail Anyone, on their phone, between meetings The single number they came to check Phone layout with that number pinned at the top (see Mobile, above) The same underlying model can serve both — an executive summary page built from cards and a KPI trend, and a detail page built from a full Matrix, linked by a button (see Interactivity ). Building one page and hoping it satisfies both audiences is how a report ends up too sparse for the analyst and too dense for the executive at the same time. The one-line test: before shipping any report, ask whether a first-time viewer — someone who has never seen this data before — could look at each chart for five seconds and correctly state what it's telling them. If not, the fix is almost always on this page: a truncated axis, a missing title, decorative color, or clutter that needs removing. For each one that fails, note which specific rule from this page it's breaking (truncated axis? default title? no display units?) and fix it. title: Interactivity
headings: A dashboard that responds is worth ten that don't.
text: Module 2 · Interactivity A dashboard that responds is worth ten that don't. Every feature on this page turns a static picture into something a viewer can actually explore — click deeper, jump to detail, save a view, tell a story across pages. All of it is on-canvas navigation: nothing here requires leaving Power BI or writing DAX. Exploring one visual Drill-down Concept: Clicking deeper into the SAME hierarchy on the SAME visual — Category → Sub-Category → Product, one chart, three levels. Why it matters: One chart answers "what's the total" and "what's inside that total" without building three separate charts. Real-world example: A retail category manager sees Electronics is the top category, drills in, and finds Laptops are carrying nearly all of it — Headphones barely sell. Steps Build a Bar or Column chart with a multi-level field well: drag Category, then Sub Category, into the same Axis well (Power BI treats this as a hierarchy automatically) Turn on the drill icons in the visual header (the down-arrow and the double-down "expand" icon) Click a bar, then click the single down-arrow to drill into just that category Click the up-arrow to drill back up Try it below — this is a real, clickable mock of the mechanic, not a screenshot: ← Back to Category Category Click a bar to drill into it. Click "Back" to drill back up — exactly the same up/down motion as the real drill icons. Common mistake: Putting unrelated fields in the same Axis well and calling it a hierarchy — Region under Product doesn't mean anything; a hierarchy needs a genuine parent-child relationship. Best practice: Keep hierarchies to 2–3 levels. Beyond that, a drill-through page (below) usually communicates better than a fourth drill level. Tooltips Concept: The small popup that appears on hover over a data point, showing extra detail without permanently occupying space on the report. Why it matters: A chart can only show so many fields before it turns into clutter — a tooltip carries the "nice to know" fields without carrying their visual weight. Real-world example: A Sales-by-Region map shows just Region and Sales at a glance, but hovering a state reveals Profit Margin and Order Count too. Steps Drag any extra field into the Tooltip well of the Visualizations pane For a richer tooltip, build a separate small report page sized "Tooltip" (Page Information → Tooltip toggle), then reference that page name in another visual's Tooltip well Best practice: Keep default tooltips to 2–4 fields. Reach for a full report-page tooltip only when hover detail genuinely needs its own mini chart. Common mistake: Relying on a tooltip to convey a number the audience needs to act on — if it's important enough to decide something, it belongs on the visual itself, not hidden behind a hover. Drill-down vs. Tooltip: Drill-down changes what the chart is SHOWING (fewer, more specific bars). A tooltip changes nothing on the chart — it only reveals extra detail for the one point being hovered, then disappears. Jumping to another view Drill-down stays on one visual and goes deeper. Drill-through leaves the page entirely. Drill-through Concept: Right-clicking a data point to jump to a completely separate, filtered detail page built specifically for that context. Why it matters: Some questions need an entirely different LAYOUT to answer — not just fewer bars on the same chart, but different visuals altogether (a customer's full order history, say). Real-world example: Right-click a customer on a Sales Overview page, choose "Drill through → Customer Detail," and land on a page built just for that one customer's order history, complaints, and lifetime value. Steps Build the detail page (e.g. "Customer Detail") Drag the field it should filter by (e.g. Customer Name) into the Drill Through well in the Format pane of that page A "Back" button appears automatically on the detail page On the source page, right-click any data point → the drill-through page appears under "Drill through" Common mistake: Forgetting the detail page still needs its own visuals built — drill-through only handles the filtering and navigation, not the page's content. Try it yourself: Build a one-page "Product Detail" report filtered by Product, drill through to it from a Bar Chart of Sales by Product. Bookmarks Concept: A saved snapshot of a report's current state — filters, visibility, selections, even scroll position — that a button can jump straight back to. Why it matters: It turns a single flexible page into several "views" without duplicating the page, and it's the engine behind interactive storytelling (below). Real-world example: A dashboard has two bookmarks — "This Year" and "Last Year" — each pre-filtering the same visuals to a different date range, one click apart. Steps Set up the report exactly how you want it captured (filters applied, visuals shown/hidden) View → Bookmarks pane → Add Name the bookmark clearly (e.g. "This Year") Repeat for each state you want to save Wire each one to a button (next lesson) Best practice: In the bookmark's options, uncheck "Data" if you only want it to control visibility/selection, not re-apply filters — the two behave very differently and it's a common source of confusion. Buttons & Navigation (Page and Report level) Concept: Buttons are clickable shapes wired to an action — most often jumping to a bookmark or another page. Navigation is the pattern of using several buttons together as a menu. Why it matters: A viewer shouldn't need to know Power BI's page tabs exist — a button labeled "Regional Detail" is self-explanatory in a way a small tab strip isn't. Real-world example: A left-hand strip of buttons — Overview, Sales, Customers, Products — turns a 4-page report into something that feels like a real app. Steps Insert → Buttons → Blank (or a built-in style) Format the button → Action → turn On Type: Page navigation (jump to a page) or Bookmark (jump to a saved state) Pick the destination page or bookmark Repeat for every destination, then duplicate the button strip onto every page for consistent navigation Common mistake: Hiding the native page tabs (View → Page Navigator off) before every page has its own way back — always leave one path home. Bookmark vs. Page navigation: Page navigation always jumps to the same fixed page. A bookmark can jump to the SAME page in a different state (different filters, different visuals shown) — or to a different page entirely with a specific state pre-applied. A bookmark is strictly more powerful; a plain page-navigation button is simpler when state doesn't matter. Tooltip vs. Drill-through: A tooltip stays on the SAME page and disappears the moment the mouse moves away — it's a glance, not a destination. Drill-through actually navigates to a different page that stays put until the viewer clicks Back. Putting it together Interactive Storytelling Concept: Combining bookmarks, buttons, and the Selection pane into a guided sequence — the report walks a viewer through a specific narrative instead of leaving them to find it themselves. Why it matters: A board presentation needs a story ("here's the problem, here's the driver, here's the recommendation"), not just a dashboard to poke at. Real-world example: Three bookmarks — "1. The Problem" (a KPI in red), "2. The Driver" (a Bar Chart appears, highlighting one region), "3. The Fix" (a target line and a written recommendation) — stepped through with Next/Back buttons during a live presentation. Steps Plan the sequence on paper first: what does the viewer see at each step, and why Build every visual for every step on the same page (Selection pane will control what's visible when) Create one bookmark per step, capturing which visuals are visible/hidden at that step Add Next/Back buttons wired to the bookmarks, or group all bookmarks into a Bookmark navigator (Insert → Buttons → Bookmark navigator) for automatic step buttons Best practice: Never more than 4–5 steps — storytelling mode is for a live walkthrough, not a replacement for the dashboard someone explores on their own later. Exercises Exercise 1 · Drill-through Build a Customer Detail page Using the Sales dataset, build a "Customer Detail" page filtered by Customer, then right-click a bar on a Sales-by-Customer chart on a separate Overview page and drill through to it. Exercise 2 · Bookmarks & Buttons A "This Year / Last Year" toggle Create two bookmarks that apply different Date filters to the same page, then wire two buttons to jump between them — no page navigation, just a state change.
