title: Tables & Matrix
headings: Sometimes a chart is the wrong answer. Sometimes the audience just wants the numbers.
Same Sales data, two shapes: Region → Category
text: Module 2 · Tables & Matrix Sometimes a chart is the wrong answer. Sometimes the audience just wants the numbers. A Table and a Matrix are Power BI's two grid visuals — no bars, no lines, just rows and columns of exact values. A Table lists rows flat, one per record, the way a spreadsheet does. A Matrix groups rows into a hierarchy and subtotals automatically, the way a PivotTable does. Same underlying data, two very different shapes — this page builds both from the same Sales rows so the difference is concrete, not theoretical. Same rows, two shapes — the worked example below builds both from real Sales data. Table Building it: columns, measures & sorting Concept: A Table visual lists one row per record in your data, with every field you drag in becoming a column — plain columns and DAX measures sit side by side with no special treatment. Real-world example: An ops manager wants a literal order log — every Order ID, who bought it, and what it made — to sanity-check the summary charts against, or to export for a follow-up email. Steps Visualizations pane → Table Drag Order ID, Customer, Region, Category, Sub Category into Columns — each adds a plain field, no aggregation Drag Sales into Columns too — a numeric column defaults to Sum, shown per row here since each row is already one order Click any column header to sort by it; click again to reverse; a small arrow shows the active sort Drag column borders in the header to resize, or drag a header left/right to reorder columns Common mistake: Dropping every available field into a Table "just in case." A Table with 15 columns forces horizontal scrolling and defeats the point — include only what the reader actually needs to check or export. Formatting: alternating rows, header style & borders Concept: The Format pane (paint-roller icon) controls how the grid itself looks, separately from the data in it — row banding, header color/font, and gridlines. Why it matters: A wide table with 20+ rows is hard to scan in a single flat color — the eye loses which row it's on. Small formatting choices carry real readability. Steps Format pane → Column headers → set font weight, background fill, and text color Format pane → Grid → turn on Row banding for alternating row colors, and pick the banded color Format pane → Grid → set vertical/horizontal gridline weight and color, or turn them off for a cleaner look Format pane → Values → adjust text size and cell padding once columns feel cramped Best practice: A subtle row band (a faint tint, not a bright color) does more for scanability than heavy borders ever will — use borders sparingly, mainly to separate the header from the data. Totals Concept: A pinned row at the bottom of the table showing one aggregation per numeric column — the same idea as an Excel SUM row, built in. Real-world example: A finance reviewer scrolling a table of 80 orders still needs the grand total of Sales and Profit visible without scrolling back to the top or building a separate KPI card. Steps Format pane → Total → toggle on (it's on by default for a new Table) Still in Total , click each numeric column's dropdown to choose its aggregation — Sum, Average, Count, Min, or Max, set independently per column Turn the toggle off entirely for a Table meant to be scanned row-by-row, where a totals row would just be noise Common mistake: Leaving every numeric column defaulted to Sum. Averaging Discount % or Credit Score and summing it instead produces a number nobody can use — check the aggregation per column, not just per table. Data bars & icons — in-cell visual cues Concept: Two ways to fold a small chart into a single cell. Data bars shade the cell background proportional to the value, showing relative magnitude without leaving the grid. Icons place a small conditional symbol — commonly an up/flat/down arrow — next to the number based on which rule it matches. Real-world example: A Sales column with data bars lets a manager spot the biggest orders at a glance, in the same table they're already reading line by line. A Profit column with icons flags which orders lost money with a red down arrow, no separate chart required. Steps Select the Table, then in the Format pane find Cell elements Turn on Data bars , pick the numeric column (e.g. Sales), and set the bar color, minimum, and maximum Turn on Icons instead (or alongside), pick the column (e.g. Profit), choose an icon set, and set the rule thresholds — e.g. below 0 = red down arrow, above 0 = green up arrow Best practice: Pick one — data bars or icons — per column, not both; stacking both in the same cell gets visually noisy fast. Conditional formatting on a Table Concept: Conditional formatting rules can also color a cell's background or font based on its value — the classic red/yellow/green pattern, applied to a whole column at once. It lives in the same Cell elements panel as data bars and icons above, and the full rule-building walkthrough — background color, font color, rules vs. gradients, applying it to one column vs. the whole table — is its own page next: Conditional Formatting . This page just flags that the option sits here, on a Table exactly like it does on a Matrix. Search within a table Concept: A magnifying-glass icon in the visual's header that filters the Table's own rows to whatever text is typed — a live find-as-you-type, scoped to that one visual. Real-world example: A support rep pulls up the order table during a customer call and types the customer's name to jump straight to their rows, instead of scrolling a hundred-row list. Steps Select the Table → Format pane → Header icons → turn on Search The magnifying-glass icon appears in the visual's top-right corner at report view (not edit view) — click it and type Common mistake: Confusing this with a report-level slicer — table search only filters that one Table visual, not the rest of the page, and it isn't saved as part of the report's state the way a bookmark or slicer selection is. Matrix Rows, Columns & Values wells Concept: A Matrix has three field wells instead of a Table's one flat Columns well. Rows groups records down the left side — drop more than one field in and it becomes a hierarchy, nested in the order you dropped them. Columns optionally spreads a field across the top instead, turning categories into their own set of columns (a true cross-tab). Values holds the numbers, always aggregated — never one row per record the way a Table shows them. Real-world example: A regional head wants Sales broken down by Region, then by Category inside each region, as a compact grid rather than one row per individual order. Field mapping Table: Sales Sales[Region] Rows (level 1) Sales[Category] Rows (level 2, nested) Sales[Sales] (Sum) Values All three fields live on the one Sales table — the full worked example is below, under "Table vs. Matrix." Steps Visualizations pane → Matrix Drag Region into Rows Drag Category into Rows too, underneath Region — Power BI nests it automatically as a second hierarchy level Drag Sales into Values — it aggregates as Sum by default Optional: drag a field like Region into Columns instead of Rows to lay Sales across the top as a true cross-tab Common mistake: Dragging a raw column (not a measure) into Values and expecting it to behave like a Table's per-row column — in a Matrix, every field in Values is aggregated, because Matrix rows represent GROUPS of records, not single records. Hierarchies & expand/collapse Concept: Stacking two or more fields in the Rows well (Region, then Category) builds a hierarchy — Power BI shows a +/- icon next to each Region row so the viewer can open it to see the Categories inside, without those rows always being on screen. Real-world example: A one-page executive view starts fully collapsed — just four Region rows and their totals. The CFO expands only the region that looks off, instead of scrolling past every Category for every Region up front. Steps Click the + icon next to a Region row to reveal just that region's Categories — "expand to next level," one branch at a time Click the − icon to collapse that branch back Right-click any row → Expand → Expand entire hierarchy to open every Region's Categories at once, in a single click Right-click → Collapse → Collapse entire hierarchy to snap everything back down to just the top level Best practice: Ship a Matrix collapsed to the top level by default (Format pane → Row headers won't remember an expanded state on refresh anyway) — let the viewer choose to drill into what they care about. Subtotals & Grand totals Concept: Because a Matrix groups rows, it can show a subtotal at each level of the hierarchy — a Region's total across all its Categories — on top of the single Grand Total across everything, at the very bottom. Real-world example: Collapsed, a Region/Category Matrix already tells the regional head each region's total Sales — that number is the Region subtotal, visible with zero clicks, before anyone expands anything. Steps Format pane → Subtotals → toggle Row subtotals on or off With multiple row levels, use Per row level to turn subtotals off for just one level (e.g. keep the Region subtotal, drop a redundant Category-only subtotal) while keeping others on Same panel → toggle Column subtotals if a field is in Columns too Grand Total is controlled separately in the same Subtotals section Common mistake: Turning off Grand Total on a report a finance audience will screenshot — losing the one number everyone checks first is a bigger problem than a slightly taller table. Stepped layout Concept: With stepped layout on (the default), each nested row level indents further right, so Category rows visually sit "inside" their Region, all sharing one row-header column. Turn it off and every hierarchy level gets its own separate, aligned column instead — Region in one column, Category in the next, side by side. Real-world example: A dense Matrix with three nested levels (Region → Category → Sub Category) can get visually cramped once stepped — indentation alone stops making the level obvious. Turning stepped layout off gives each level its own labeled column, easier to scan at that depth. Steps Select the Matrix → Format pane → Row headers Toggle Stepped layout off Adjust Stepped layout indentation instead, if keeping it on but the indent feels too wide or too narrow Best practice: Keep stepped layout on for 2-level hierarchies — it reads naturally. Consider turning it off once a hierarchy hits 3+ levels, or once viewers keep asking "which column is this indented under?" Formatting & conditional formatting on a Matrix Concept: A Matrix takes the same row banding, header style, and gridline options as a Table (Format pane → Grid / Column headers / Row headers), plus its own subtotal/Grand Total styling. Conditional formatting — background color, font color, data bars, icons — applies the same way too, in Cell elements , and can be scoped to apply across every level of the hierarchy or only the values shown at one level. The full conditional formatting workflow — rules, gradients, and the level-scoping option specific to a Matrix — is covered in depth on the next page: Conditional Formatting . Table vs. Matrix, in one line: A Table shows records. A Matrix shows groups. If the audience needs to see or export individual rows, use a Table. If the audience needs a summary that opens up on demand, use a Matrix. Same Sales data, two shapes: Region → Category Below is the same six orders from the Sales dataset ( Order ID, Customer, Region, Sales, Profit, Category, Sub Category, Date, Discount, Quantity ), built once as a flat Table and once as a Matrix grouped by Region → Category . The numbers reconcile exactly — a Matrix isn't different data, it's the same data organized differently. As a Table — one row per order Order ID Customer Region Category Sub Category Sales ORD-1042 Priya Nair West Furniture Chairs ₹12,400 ORD-1043 Rohan Mehta West Furniture Tables ₹8,900 ORD-1044 Priya Nair West Technology Phones ₹21,300 ORD-1045 Amit Shah East Furniture Chairs ₹9,600 ORD-1046 Neha Kulkarni East Technology Phones ₹15,750 ORD-1047 Amit Shah East Technology Accessories ₹4,200 Total ₹72,150 Six rows in, six rows out — every order stays individually visible. The Totals row (above) is the only aggregation on the whole visual; there's no way to see "just West" without adding a filter or slicer. As a Matrix — grouped & subtotaled Region Category Sales West Furniture ₹21,300 Technology ₹21,300 West Total ₹42,600 East Furniture ₹9,600 Technology ₹19,950 East Total ₹29,550 Grand Total ₹72,150 Six orders collapse into 2 Region groups and 4 Region-Category groups, each summed automatically. Collapsed to just Region (click − on each), a viewer would see only West / East / Grand Total — three lines instead of six. Notice what changed and what didn't: the Grand Total is ₹72,150 in both — same underlying rows, so the math has to agree. What changed is the SHAPE: the Table can't hide Priya Nair's two West orders without a filter; the Matrix hides and reveals them on click, and adds two subtotal rows the Table has no equivalent for at all. Exercise Practice · Table & Matrix HR dataset — build both, compare Build a flat Table of the HR dataset (Employee ID, Department, Location, Salary), then build a Matrix with Department in Rows, Location in Columns, and Average Salary in Values. Which one answers "who has the highest salary" faster? Which one answers "how does average salary vary by department and location" faster? Module 2 · Tables & Matrix Next: Conditional Formatting →

title: Conditional Formatting
headings: Color does the reading so the executive doesn't have to.
Thresholds — fixed number vs. a field that defines it
Try it — same number, colored by a different measure
Banking dataset — flag the risky loans
text: Module 2 · Conditional Formatting Color does the reading so the executive doesn't have to. Conditional formatting changes a visual's color, font, bar, or icon based on the value itself — the exact same trick as Excel's Conditional Formatting, just applied to a card, table, or matrix instead of a spreadsheet range. A busy VP shouldn't have to read 40 rows of a table to find the one that's a problem. Color should find it for them. Where the dialog lives Conditional formatting is set per-field, on a table, matrix, or card-style visual — not on the visual as a whole. There are two doors into the same dialog: Select the visual → Values well → click the ▾ next to the field → Conditional formatting → pick a rule type Select the visual → Format pane (paint roller) → Cell elements → toggle a rule type on → click fx Both paths open the same dialog box. The field dropdown is faster once you know a field needs formatting; the Format pane's Cell elements section is where you go to see — or turn off — every rule already applied to a visual. The analytical point, not just the technical one: a table of 200 rows makes every number look equally important. Conditional formatting is the only feature on this site whose entire job is to make the UNimportant rows fade and the exceptions — the ones actually worth a decision — visually shout. That's the reason it exists, not decoration. Every formatting type on this page is the same three-step idea underneath. The formatting types All seven live in the same dialog, under a "Format style" dropdown. Click any card for steps and an example. Background color rules Concept: Fills the entire cell background with a color determined by that cell's value — either a smooth gradient across the range, or a fixed color once a value crosses a threshold. Real-world example: A Profit table where every negative-profit row gets a solid red cell background — impossible to scroll past without noticing. Steps Click the field's ▾ in the Values well → Conditional formatting → Background color Format style: Gradient (gradient across the range) or Rules (fixed color bands) Pick the field the color should be BASED ON — usually the same field, but it doesn't have to be Apply Best practice: Keep the fill readable — dark backgrounds need a light font color or the number disappears into its own cell. Font color rules Concept: The same rule engine as Background color, but it recolors just the text — the cell itself stays the table's normal background. Real-world example: A dense Sales table where only the number turns red for a below-target row, keeping the table visually quiet everywhere else — useful when a full-cell fill would feel too loud for a page with many other colored elements. Steps Field's ▾ → Conditional formatting → Font color Same Gradient / Rules choice as Background color Apply Best practice: Use Font color instead of Background color when a table already has other color elements (icons, data bars) and a full cell fill would start to compete with them. Data bars Concept: A small in-cell horizontal bar, drawn behind the number, sized relative to the column's minimum and maximum — a miniature bar chart living inside a table cell. Real-world example: A Regional Sales table where every row shows both the exact number AND a bar — so North's bar visibly dwarfs West's, without building a separate chart. Steps Field's ▾ → Conditional formatting → Data bars Set Minimum and Maximum (leave on "Automatic" to use the column's own lowest/highest value) Optionally turn off "Show bar only" if you want the bar with no number at all — usually leave it off so the exact figure stays visible Apply Best practice: Data bars are the fastest way to make a plain table feel like a chart without leaving the table visual — reach for them before building a separate bar chart next to it. Icons Concept: A small icon placed next to the value — arrows (up/flat/down), traffic lights (red/yellow/green circles), or stars — chosen from a preset icon set based on which threshold band the value falls into. Real-world example: A KPI table where every metric gets a traffic-light icon: green circle for on-target, yellow for close, red for missed — readable from across a conference room, before anyone reads a single digit. Steps Field's ▾ → Conditional formatting → Icons Pick an icon set (arrows, traffic lights, ratings, etc.) Set the thresholds for each icon band, and where the icon sits (Left of value is the default) Apply Best practice: Traffic lights read fastest for status (good/warning/bad); arrows read fastest for direction of change (up/down vs. last period). Pick the set that matches the QUESTION, not just what looks nice. Rules-based formatting Concept: Explicit if/then bands you define yourself — "if value 10 then red," "if value is between 10 and 20 then yellow," "if value 20 then green" — instead of a smooth gradient. Available under the Rules format style for Background color, Font color, and Icons alike. Real-world example: "If Profit Margin % 10% then red background" — a hard line a finance team actually uses to flag a product for review, not a vague "redder = worse" gradient. Steps Field's ▾ → Conditional formatting → Background color (or Font color / Icons) Format style: Rules Click "+ New rule" for each band, setting the comparison ("is less than," "is between," etc.) and the color for that band Apply Best practice: Reach for Rules whenever the business already has a named threshold ("below 10% margin is a problem") — a gradient can't express a hard line the way an explicit rule can. Color scales Concept: A continuous gradient from one color to another (often through a middle color) spread smoothly across the field's full range — the "Gradient" format style, as opposed to the hard bands of Rules-based formatting. Real-world example: A Profit Margin column shaded on a red → yellow → green gradient — a 4% margin renders as a deep red cell, an 11% margin as a pale yellow-green, a 22% margin as a solid green, with every value in between shaded proportionally, not sorted into three flat buckets. Steps Field's ▾ → Conditional formatting → Background color Format style: Gradient Set Minimum color, (optional) Center color, and Maximum color Apply Color scale vs. Rules — same dialog, different feel: a color scale shows every shade of the story (a 9% margin looks slightly different from an 11% margin). Rules-based formatting collapses that nuance into a small number of named bands (red / yellow / green) so a value is either "in the problem group" or it isn't. Use a scale to see the whole distribution; use Rules to draw a line a decision gets made against. Formatting by a measure, not the raw column Concept: Every dialog above has a "Based on field" dropdown — and it does NOT have to be the same field being displayed. You can color one visible value using an entirely different, independently calculated measure . Why it matters: A raw Sales number, on its own, has no opinion about whether it's good or bad — 4.2 million could be a triumph or a disaster depending on what it's being compared to. A separate measure can carry that comparison (e.g. Sales vs Target % ), and the KPI card showing raw Sales can borrow that measure's verdict for its color, without displaying the measure itself anywhere on the page. Real-world example: A "Total Sales" card shows ₹42.8L in plain black-on-white — a perfectly correct number that tells a viewer nothing about whether it's a good month. Point its Background color rule at a hidden Sales vs Target % measure instead of at Sales itself, and the exact same card turns green when the number is ahead of target and red when it's behind — the visible number never changes, only what decides its color does. Steps Write the DAX measure first — e.g. Sales vs Target % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Target Sales], [Target Sales]) Select the visual → field's ▾ → Conditional formatting → Background color (or Font color / Icons) In "Based on field," change it from the displayed field to the new measure Set the rule/gradient against the MEASURE's range (e.g. below 0% = red), not the displayed number's range Common mistake: Leaving "Based on field" pointed at the same field that's displayed, then wondering why a KPI can only ever be colored by its own raw size — never by whether that size is actually good or bad. Thresholds — fixed number vs. a field that defines it Fixed threshold A hard-coded number typed straight into the rule — "if value 10 then red." Simple, and correct for a genuinely fixed business line. Example: A hospital compliance rule of "on-time discharge = processed within 5 days" that regulators define once and don't change often. Weakness: if the threshold ever needs to change, someone has to reopen the dialog and edit the rule by hand, on every visual that used it. Dynamic threshold (a field or measure) The cutoff itself comes from data — a Target column, or a measure like [Target Sales] — instead of a number typed into the dialog. Example: Each region has its own Target Sales value; a single "Sales vs Target %" measure divides actual by that region's own target, so the SAME rule correctly flags North against North's goal and South against South's — no per-region rule needed. Strength: update the underlying Target data and every visual using that measure re-evaluates automatically — nobody touches the formatting rule itself. Rule of thumb: if the business would ever say "well, it depends" when asked what the threshold should be, it depends on something — put that something in a measure, don't hard-code a single number that's secretly wrong for half the rows. Try it — same number, colored by a different measure Four region KPI cards below all show Total Sales — the number never changes. What changes their color is a separate, hidden measure: Sales vs Target % , using fixed Rules-based thresholds (below 0% = red, 0–5% = amber, above 5% = green). Click a month to simulate a data refresh and watch the SAME cards recolor as the underlying measure moves — nothing about how Sales itself is displayed changes. Month 1 Month 2 Month 3 Each card's badge shows the hidden measure driving its color — that measure is never displayed as its own visual, only used to decide red / amber / green. Highlighting exceptions — the actual point Every technique above is in service of one analytical goal: a viewer should be able to glance at a table of 50, 200, or 2,000 rows and instantly know which handful need attention — without reading every single number. That's not a formatting nicety, it's the difference between a report someone actually uses every morning and one they open once and never trust again. Five business examples Scenario Before (no formatting) After (conditional formatting) Revenue vs. target Sales dataset, by Region A plain number per region — a viewer has to already know each region's target from memory to judge it. Background color Rules on a Sales vs Target % measure — green above target, red below. on target behind Profit margin Sales dataset, Profit ÷ Sales A column of percentages, all the same plain black text — a 3% margin and a 30% margin look equally routine. Color scale (Gradient), red low → green high, so the eye sorts the whole column by shade before reading a single number. SLA / turnaround time Hospital dataset, Admission Date → Discharge Date A Length-of-Stay column of raw day counts — nothing marks which admissions blew past an acceptable turnaround. Icons (traffic light) driven by a % Within SLA measure — e.g. discharged within 5 days = green, 6–7 = yellow, 8+ = red — flags exactly which patients' stays ran long. Data quality scores callback to Power Query A cleaned table looks uniformly trustworthy — but some rows started with 4 issues fixed automatically and some with none; that history is invisible after the fact. Rules-based background color on an "Issues Fixed" count column — 0 issues plain, 1–2 amber, 3+ red — so a reviewer can spot-check the rows that needed the most repair, exactly the trims/typos/blanks covered on the Power Query page. Regional performance Sales / Retail dataset, Region column A table of Region + Sales — comparing four numbers means reading each one and doing the ranking in your head. Data bars on the Sales column — North's bar visibly dwarfs West's at a glance, no mental math required. Common mistakes Formatting everything Conditional formatting on every single column turns a table into a rainbow with no clear signal — reserve it for the 1–3 fields that actually drive a decision. Red/green with no legend A viewer new to the report has no way to know red means "below target" versus "above budget" versus something else — a one-line caption or consistent site-wide convention (red = bad) removes the ambiguity. Coloring the raw value when the verdict lives elsewhere Leaving "Based on field" pointed at the same displayed column means the color can only ever reflect that number's own size — not whether it's actually good, which usually depends on a target or comparison the raw value alone can't express. Hard-coding a threshold that varies by group Typing one fixed number when the real cutoff differs by region, department, or product silently misjudges every group whose true target isn't that number — a measure-based threshold fixes this once, everywhere. Best practice: Before opening the dialog, answer one question: "what should a viewer DO differently when they see red versus green?" If there's no clear answer, the formatting is decoration, not analysis — skip it. Apply a color scale to Credit Score (red low, green high), and a rules-based background color to Loan Status (red for "Rejected," green for "Approved"). Which rows would a credit officer look at first? title: Filters
headings: Retail dataset — three scopes, one page
text: Module 2 · Filters Same filter, three different reaches. A filter restricts which rows are included — the only real decision is how FAR that restriction should reach: one visual, one page, or the whole report. The three scopes Visual-level filter Affects: one specific visual only. When to use: one chart needs to show something different from everything else on the page — e.g. a "Top 5 Products" table that should stay Top 5 even while the rest of the page shows all products. Example: A Filters pane filter applied with that one visual selected. Page-level filter Affects: every visual on the current page. When to use: the whole page is about one slice of the business — a "2025 Only" page, or a page dedicated to one region. Example: Set once at the Page level in the Filters pane; every visual added to that page inherits it automatically. Report-level filter Affects: every visual on every page of the report. When to use: a restriction that should never be bypassed anywhere — e.g. excluding test/dummy data, or scoping an entire report to one business unit. Example: Set at the Report level in the Filters pane — the broadest, least common scope. The rule of reach: Visual filter → one visual. Page filter → every visual on that page (including ones added later). Report filter → every visual on every page (including pages added later). Higher scopes are inherited automatically — a page filter doesn't need to be repeated per visual. Three nested scopes — a filter set anywhere is inherited by everything inside it. See the reach — interactive Three mock visuals below: A and B live on this page, C represents a visual on a different page of the same report. Apply the same "Category = Electronics" filter at each scope and watch which ones respond. Apply: Visual filter (on A only) Apply: Page filter (this page) Apply: Report filter (whole report) Clear Visual A · this page No filter applied Visual B · this page No filter applied Visual C · Page 2 No filter applied Notice the Visual filter only ever marks A. The Page filter marks A and B, never C. Only the Report filter reaches all three — including the one on another page. Common mistakes Wrong scope, right value Setting a filter at Report level "to be safe" when only one visual needed it — now every future page inherits a restriction nobody remembers adding. Forgetting inherited filters exist A number looks wrong on one visual, but the real culprit is a Page or Report filter set weeks ago, not the visual itself — always check all three panes (Visual, Page, Report) in the Filters pane before debugging the DAX. Best practice: Default to the narrowest scope that solves the problem. It's much easier to notice and widen a Visual filter later than to hunt down a forgotten Report filter across a dozen pages. Exercise Practice · Filters Retail dataset — three scopes, one page Build a page with 3 visuals from the Retail dataset. Apply a Visual filter (Product = a single product) to just one of them, then apply a Page filter (Date = current year) that affects all three. Explain in one sentence why you chose each scope for each filter. title: Slicers & Synced Slicers
headings: Hand the viewer a filter they can click, not one you set for them.
Slicer vs. Filters pane — who's actually in control
When to reach for a slicer
Matching the slicer to the data type
Sync Slicers — one control, every page
Two pages, one synced Region slicer
text: Module 2 · Slicers Hand the viewer a filter they can click, not one you set for them. A slicer is a filter left out in the open — an on-canvas control the report VIEWER clicks, instead of a restriction the report BUILDER locks in once behind the Filters pane. Slicer vs. Filters pane — who's actually in control The Filters page covered visual, page, and report-level filters — all of them set once by the BUILDER, invisible to whoever opens the report. A slicer is different in one specific way: it puts that same filtering power directly on the canvas, so the VIEWER can change it themselves, any time, without ever opening a menu. Filter (Filters pane) Slicer (on-canvas) Who sets it The report builder, at design time The report viewer, at any time Who can change it Only someone editing the report Anyone viewing the report Where it lives Tucked away in a side pane A visible tile, right on the report Best for A restriction that should never move Letting someone self-serve their own slice Same engine, different owner: a slicer isn't a new filtering mechanism — it's a visual, and visuals can be filtered just like any other visual. The difference is purely who gets to touch the control. When to reach for a slicer Use a slicer whenever a business user needs to answer "show me just my region" or "just my team" without knowing Power BI exists underneath. If the answer to "who decides the filter value" is "whoever happens to be looking at the report right now," it's a slicer — not a Filters-pane filter. Real-world example: A regional sales manager in the North opens the same company-wide report every Monday. Nobody is going to rebuild the report just for her — a Region slicer lets her click "North" once and every visual on the page instantly reflects only her territory. Creating a slicer Visualizations pane → Slicer icon → drag a field into the Field well Click an empty area of the canvas so nothing else is selected In the Visualizations pane, click the Slicer icon to place a blank slicer Drag the field you want a viewer to filter by (e.g. Region) into the slicer's Field well Resize and position it — usually along the top or left edge, where a viewer expects controls to live List vs. dropdown List Every value shown at once, stacked vertically (or horizontally). Takes more canvas space but lets a viewer see every option and the current selection in one glance. Use when: the field has a short list of values — Region (North/South/East/West) is a textbook case. default choice for short lists Dropdown Collapses to a single line until clicked. Saves real estate but hides the current selection until the viewer looks closely at the header text. Use when: canvas space is tight, or the field has more values than comfortably fit as a list — e.g. a Sub Category field with a dozen entries. Switch between them in the Format pane → Slicer settings → Options → Style, or from the small dropdown-arrow icon in the slicer's own header. Matching the slicer to the data type Date slicer Drag a Date field in and the slicer offers a Between range, a Before/After cut-off, or a draggable slider style instead of a list of individual dates. Example: Filtering the Sales dataset's Date column to a specific order window. Numeric slicer Drag a numeric field in and the slicer becomes a range slider with two handles, instead of a list of every distinct number. Example: A Loan Amount slicer on the Banking dataset, dragged to ₹1,00,000–₹50,00,000, isolating only mid-to-large loans. Relative date filtering Instead of a fixed range that goes stale, a relative filter says "last 30 days" or "this quarter" — it recalculates itself against today's date on every refresh. Example: An operations dashboard filtered to "last 30 days" of orders never needs to be touched again — it's automatically current every Monday morning. Fixed range vs. relative: a Between filter of "1 Jan 2025 – 31 Jan 2025" is frozen forever — next month it's showing the wrong period unless someone manually updates it. A Relative Date filter of "this month" needs no maintenance at all; that's the whole point of reaching for it. Formatting a slicer Select the slicer, open the Format pane (the paint-roller icon), and the options that matter most for a beginner are: Setting What it controls Orientation Vertical (stacked list) or Horizontal (a row of chips) — horizontal suits a short Region-style list placed along the top of a page. Header Toggles the small title bar showing the field name on/off — turn it off only when the slicer's purpose is already obvious from its position or a text label nearby. Style Tile, Dropdown, Between, or Slider — the available options change automatically depending on whether the field is text, date, or numeric. Multi-select and search Multi-select By default, clicking a new value in a slicer replaces the old selection. Hold Ctrl while clicking to select several values at once, or click the small multi-select icon in the slicer's header to make every click additive without needing Ctrl. Example: Selecting both North and East on a Region slicer to compare two territories side by side. Search within a slicer A small magnifying-glass icon that turns a long list into a searchable box, so a viewer can type instead of scrolling. Example: The practice Sales file only has 33 customers, but a real company's customer table often runs into the hundreds — that's exactly when Search stops being a nice-to-have and becomes essential. Sync Slicers — one control, every page A slicer lives visually on one page. Sync Slicers (View → Sync Slicers pane) lets that slicer's selection apply its filter to OTHER pages too — even pages where the slicer itself isn't shown. Tick a page's Sync box to have it obey the selection; tick its Visible box as well if you also want the slicer control to physically appear there. Not the same as a Report-level filter: a Report filter (see the Filters page ) also reaches every page — but it's fixed by the BUILDER and the viewer can't touch it. A synced slicer reaches multiple pages too, but stays a live control the VIEWER can change at any time. Same reach, completely different owner. Real-world example: A Region slicer sits on a report's "Overview" page. With Sync Slicers turned on for the "Regional Detail" page, clicking "South" on Overview instantly re-filters Regional Detail too — one click, both pages, no second slicer to build or keep in sync by hand. One slicer, several pages, one selection kept in sync automatically. Try it below — a real, clickable mock of the mechanic, not a screenshot. Two pages of the same report, one Region slicer. Toggle Sync on and off and watch what happens to the second page: Sync: ON Sync: OFF Region slicer: North South East West Overview page · slicer lives here Region: North Regional Detail page Region: North With Sync ON, clicking a region updates both pages together. Switch Sync OFF, click a different region, and only the Overview page moves — Regional Detail freezes on its last selection until Sync is switched back on. Common mistakes Confusing sync with visibility Sync and Visible are two separate checkboxes in the Sync Slicers pane. A page can obey the synced filter (Sync ✓) without ever showing the slicer control itself (Visible unchecked) — useful when you want the effect everywhere but the control cluttering only one page. One slicer per field, everywhere Building a separate Region slicer on every page instead of syncing one is extra work and a maintenance trap — two "Region" slicers can silently drift out of agreement if a viewer only clicks one of them. Best practice: Build one slicer per field, put it on the page a viewer lands on first, and use Sync Slicers to extend its reach — don't duplicate the control across pages just to get the same filtering effect everywhere. Exercise Practice · Slicers Two pages, one synced Region slicer Build "Overview" and "Regional Detail" pages from the Retail dataset. Place a Region slicer on Overview only, then turn on Sync Slicers so Regional Detail obeys it without showing the control. Confirm clicking a region on Overview updates both pages. headings: Make it interactive — five features, one AdventureWorksDW report
text: Module 2 · Assignment Make it interactive — five features, one AdventureWorksDW report Same database as the rest of Module 1–2, one small report page — but now it has to respond when someone clicks on it. This is the assignment that separates "I can build a chart" from "I can build a report." Worth 10 marks. Individual submission, through the LMS portal. Builds on AdventureWorksDW (the same database from the SQL Server & AdventureWorks page) — no DAX measures required anywhere in this assignment, that's Module 3. Every task below is achievable with drag-and-drop field wells and built-in aggregations (Sum/Average/Count) only. The brief Using your restored AdventureWorksDW database, build a single report page in Power BI Desktop that completes all five tasks below. Unlike the Visualizations page's worked examples, tasks in this assignment are free to pull from both DimProduct and FactInternetSales together — that's the whole point of a star schema, and exactly what Module 2's Interactivity and cross-filtering lessons are testing. If a visual mixing the two tables shows blank or wrong numbers: open Model view (left-hand rail in Power BI Desktop) and confirm a relationship line connects DimProduct[ProductKey] to FactInternetSales[ProductKey] . Power BI usually autodetects it on load; if it didn't, drag one ProductKey column onto the other to create the relationship manually. The five tasks # Task Skills from 1 Build a report page with a Bar Chart (Sum of FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] by DimProduct[ProductLine] ) and a KPI Card (Sum of FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] ), plus a Slicer on DimProduct[Color] . Click a color in the slicer and confirm both other visuals cross-filter. Interactivity, Slicers 2 Build a Matrix : Rows = DimProduct[ProductLine] , Values = Count of ProductKey , Average of ListPrice , Average of StandardCost . Apply conditional formatting (a background color scale) to the Average List Price column. Tables & Matrix, Conditional Formatting 3 Build a Bar Chart of DimProduct[EnglishProductName] by ListPrice , then apply a Top N filter (Filters pane → Top N → 5, ranked by List Price) so only the 5 most expensive products show. Filters 4 Add one custom visual from AppSource (Get more visuals) and build it against any AdventureWorksDW field(s) of your choice — a Word Cloud of product names is an easy safe choice, but pick whichever one actually fits what you're showing. Custom Visuals 5 Choose one : Group DimProduct[Color] 's individual colors into 3–4 broader buckets of your own naming (e.g. Neutral / Bright / Other) and chart the grouped field — or build a Histogram of DimProduct[ListPrice] with a bin size you choose and justify. Groups & Histograms All five can live on one page, or be spread across a couple of pages — your call, as long as every task is present and working somewhere in the file. Deliverable checklist ✓ Connected live to your restored AdventureWorksDW database (not a CSV export of it) ✓ All 5 tasks present and functioning ✓ Slicer cross-filtering demonstrably works — click it and the other visuals visibly react ✓ Conditional formatting rule is visible in the Matrix, not just configured and invisible ✓ Real chart titles throughout — no default "Sum of SalesAmount by ProductLine" left on screen ✓ One consistent Theme applied across the whole page Grading rubric Criterion Marks Task 1 — Slicer + cross-filtering, demonstrably working 2 Task 2 — Matrix with correct aggregations + visible conditional formatting 2 Task 3 — Top N filter correctly applied and ranked 2 Task 4 — Custom visual added and mapped to a sensible field 1 Task 5 — Grouping or Histogram, correctly built either way 1 Design judgment — real titles, consistent theme, readable labels, sensible layout (this is graded separately from "did it technically work") 1 Submission format followed exactly (see below) 1 Total 10 How to submit Two files, exact naming, both to the LMS portal: Your Power BI file, saved and submitted as YourFullName_Module2.pbix — e.g. Anjali_Kumar_Module2.pbix A single PDF containing a full-page screenshot of every visual, plus one screenshot showing the slicer mid-click (a color selected, other visuals visibly filtered), submitted as YourFullName_Module2_Screenshots.pdf Capturing the "mid-click" screenshot: click a color in your slicer, then screenshot before clicking anywhere else — this is the one piece of evidence a static file can't show any other way, so don't skip it. title: DAX Basics & Measures
headings: DAX: Excel formulas' cousin, built for whole tables
Calculated Column vs. Measure — the first fork in the road
text: Module 3 · 1 DAX: Excel formulas' cousin, built for whole tables DAX is how you create numbers that don't already exist as a column — everything from a simple sum to a full year-over-year comparison. This page is a placeholder — full lesson content lands here as the class reaches this module. The framing below is real; the guided walkthrough, exercises, and quiz questions are still to come. Calculated Column vs. Measure — the first fork in the road Calculated Column Computed once, row by row, and physically stored in the table — like adding a new column in Excel with a formula dragged down every row. Example: Full Name = [First Name] & " " & [Last Name] — one fixed value per row, doesn't change based on what's filtered on screen. Measure Computed on the fly, only when a visual asks for it — recalculates instantly based on whatever's currently filtered/sliced. Example: Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Sales]) — the same measure returns a different number for "2025" than for "2024," automatically. The rule of thumb this module will build toward: if the number should change when someone clicks a slicer, it's almost always a measure, not a calculated column. What this page will cover 1 DAX syntax basics. Functions, operators, referencing a column with Table[Column] vs. a measure with [Measure Name] . 2 Writing your first measure. Step-by-step in the Modeling ribbon, from New Measure to seeing it work on a Card visual. 3 Common early mistakes. Using a calculated column where a measure was needed (and the performance cost of getting that backwards at scale). Module 3 · DAX Basics & Measures Next: Time Intelligence & Aggregations →

title: Time Intelligence & Aggregations
headings: "So far this year" is a formula, not a filter you set by hand
Aggregation functions — the basics that show up everywhere
Time intelligence — the same measure, a different time window
text: Module 3 · 2 "So far this year" is a formula, not a filter you set by hand Time intelligence functions and aggregation functions are the two DAX building blocks you'll reach for most often, in almost every real report. This page is a placeholder — full lesson content lands here as the class reaches this module. The framing below is real; the guided walkthrough, exercises, and quiz questions are still to come. Aggregation functions — the basics that show up everywhere Function Does what Example SUM Adds up a numeric column Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Sales]) AVERAGE Mean of a numeric column Avg Order Value = AVERAGE(Sales[Sales]) COUNT / COUNTROWS Counts rows (with/without a specific column) Order Count = COUNTROWS(Sales) DISTINCTCOUNT Counts unique values only Unique Customers = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[Customer]) Time intelligence — the same measure, a different time window YTD (Year-to-Date), MTD (Month-to-Date), and QTD (Quarter-to-Date) all answer the same shape of question: "total so far, within the current period" — without hand-typing a date range that goes stale the moment the calendar turns over. Sales YTD = TOTALYTD ( SUM (Sales[Sales]), Sales[Date]) Why this needs a real Date table: Time intelligence functions rely on a proper, continuous Date column marked as a Date table in the model — the same "Date column typed as text sorts wrong" trap already covered on the Power Query and Visualizations pages resurfaces here, with higher stakes. What this page will cover 1 Building a proper Date table. The prerequisite every time intelligence function silently assumes exists. 2 YTD, MTD, QTD side by side. One dataset, three formulas, one Line Chart comparing all three. 3 Prior-period comparisons. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and the "vs. last year" card every executive dashboard has. title: Context & Dynamic Measures
headings: The same formula, a different answer — because of context
text: Module 3 · 3 The same formula, a different answer — because of context The single hardest DAX concept to get comfortable with, and the one that makes everything after it click: a measure has no fixed value — its answer depends entirely on what's currently filtering it. This page is a placeholder — full lesson content lands here as the class reaches this module. The framing below is real; the guided walkthrough, exercises, and quiz questions are still to come. Row context vs. Filter context Row context "Which row am I on right now?" — active inside a calculated column (evaluated once per row) and inside iterator functions like SUMX . Filter context "What's currently sliced/filtered?" — the region clicked on a map, the year picked on a slicer, even the row a Matrix visual happens to be rendering. A measure re-evaluates fresh inside whatever filter context surrounds it. This is exactly why a Total Sales measure shows a different number on every row of a Region-by-Category Matrix, and yet is written only ONCE — the formula never changes, only the filter context around it does. The single hardest thing to internalize about DAX: the formula is constant, the context around it isn't — so the answer isn't either. Dynamic measures with IF Wrapping a measure in IF lets it change WHAT it calculates based on a condition, not just format the same number differently. Status Flag = IF ([Total Sales] [Target], "On Track" , "Behind" ) What this page will cover 1 Seeing filter context change live. The same card, clicking through slicers, watching the number update — before writing a single new formula. 2 Row context inside SUMX. When a plain SUM isn't enough because the calculation itself varies row by row (e.g. Qty × Unit Price before summing). 3 Dynamic measure-switching. Using a field parameter or disconnected table + SWITCH to let a report viewer pick which measure a chart shows. Module 3 · Context & Dynamic Measures Next: CALCULATE, FILTER & Modeling →

title: CALCULATE, FILTER & Modeling
headings: CALCULATE: the one function that changes everything else
Relationships and data modeling best practices
text: Module 3 · 4 CALCULATE: the one function that changes everything else CALCULATE is the function that lets a measure override its own filter context on purpose — arguably the single most important function in all of DAX. This page is a placeholder — full lesson content lands here as the class reaches this module. The framing below is real; the guided walkthrough, exercises, and quiz questions are still to come. CALCULATE and FILTER Electronics Sales = CALCULATE ( SUM (Sales[Sales]), Sales[Category] = "Electronics" ) Read this as: "Compute SUM(Sales[Sales]) , but first override the filter context so only Category = Electronics rows count — regardless of what the report's own slicers currently say." That override is the entire trick, and everything from "Approval Rate" on the Cheat Sheet page to a proper YTD calculation is built on it. Every DAX example already on this site that uses CALCULATE — Approved Loans, Length of Stay comparisons — is doing exactly this: computing a number under a DELIBERATELY different condition than whatever's currently on screen. Relationships and data modeling best practices None of the above works without a correctly built relationship between tables — the same Data Model concept from the Architecture page, revisited with the modeling discipline a real project needs. Star schema , not a web One central fact table, dimension tables branching off it — never dimension-to-dimension relationships if a fact table can sit between them instead. Cardinality matters Relationships should run from the "many" side (a fact table, many rows per customer) to the "one" side (a dimension table, one row per customer) — get this backwards and totals silently multiply. What this page will cover 1 CALCULATE, step by step. Building up from a single filter argument to multiple combined conditions. 2 FILTER as a table function. When a simple column condition isn't enough and CALCULATE needs a more complex FILTER expression instead. 3 A full data model, built from scratch. Taking the Sales, HR, and Retail practice datasets and correctly relating them into one star-schema model. Module 3 · CALCULATE, FILTER & Modeling Next: Module 3 Assignment →

title: Module 3 Assignment
headings: Five measures, each one number harder than the last
Before you write a single measure
text: Module 3 · Assignment Five measures, each one number harder than the last DAX is a skill you build by writing formulas that break, then fixing them — not by reading about them. All five measures below use only functions this module covers: SUM, DIVIDE, TOTALYTD, CALCULATE, and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR. Worth 10 marks. Individual submission, through the LMS portal. Built on AdventureWorksDW, same database as every module so far. Before you write a single measure Mark DimDate as a Date Table first. TOTALYTD and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR (Tasks 3 and 5) silently assume this — without it they either error or quietly return wrong numbers. In Model view: select DimDate → Table tools ribbon → Mark as Date Table → point it at DimDate[FullDateAlternateKey] . Confirm a relationship line already connects FactInternetSales[OrderDateKey] to DimDate[DateKey] — if it's missing, create it in Model view before continuing. The five measures # Measure Business question it answers 1 A plain aggregation: Total Sales , summing FactInternetSales[SalesAmount] "How much have we sold, total?" 2 A ratio using DIVIDE : Profit Margin % , from SalesAmount and TotalProductCost "Of every rupee of sales, how much is actually profit?" 3 A time-intelligence measure using TOTALYTD : Sales YTD "How are we doing so far this year?" 4 A CALCULATE + column-filter measure: Road Bike Sales , filtered to DimProduct[ProductLine] = "R" "How much of our total is from Road bikes specifically, regardless of what's sliced on screen?" 5 A CALCULATE + SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR measure: Sales Same Period Last Year "Is this actually growth, or does last year look the same?" What actually gets graded For every measure, submit two things, not one: the formula itself, and a single plain-English sentence explaining what its filter context is doing at the moment it calculates. That sentence is the actual MBA-level skill here — anyone can copy a DIVIDE formula off a table; explaining why Measure 4 ignores whatever Category slicer is on the page, in your own words, is what the marks are for. Example of the explanation we want (this one won't earn marks — it's for Measure 4, already given away above): "Road Bike Sales always filters to ProductLine = R first, then sums SalesAmount within that — so it shows the same number whether or not a viewer has clicked a different ProductLine in a slicer elsewhere on the page." Five sentences like that, one per measure, are worth as much as the formulas themselves. Deliverable checklist ✓ DimDate correctly marked as a Date Table, relationship to FactInternetSales confirmed ✓ All 5 measures written and showing correct, sensible values on a Card or Table visual ✓ One written sentence per measure explaining its filter context, in your own words ✓ No calculated columns used where a measure was the right call — this module's whole point Grading rubric Criterion Marks Measures 1–2 (aggregation, ratio) — correct and sensible 2 Measure 3 (TOTALYTD) — Date table marked correctly, formula works 2 Measure 4 (CALCULATE + filter) — correct, ignores page-level slicers as intended 2 Measure 5 (CALCULATE + SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR) — correct 2 Five filter-context explanations — accurate, in your own words, not copy-pasted 2 Total 10 How to submit Two files, exact naming, both to the LMS portal: Your Power BI file, saved and submitted as YourFullName_Module3.pbix A single PDF with a screenshot of all 5 measures' DAX formulas (Modeling → the measure → formula bar, or the Measure list) plus your 5 written explanations, submitted as YourFullName_Module3_Writeup.pdf Module 3 · Assignment Next: Power Query Editor →

title: Power Query Editor
headings: Real data is never clean. This is where you fix it.
text:
Module 4 · 1 Real data is never clean. This is where you fix it. Some analysts spend 70–80% of their time right here, not in charts. All 25 lessons below run on real practice files — mostly PQ_Practice_Orders.csv , plus its two companion tables for combining data and the original Sales_Dirty.csv for a few classics. Download them from the Datasets page and follow along. Transformation Fixes Where to click Rename Columns Cryptic or abbreviated headers Double-click the column header Remove Columns Unused clutter columns Right-click header → Remove Split Column One column secretly holding two values ("Bangalore, Karnataka") Select column → Split Column → By Delimiter Merge Columns Two columns that need to become one (First + Last Name) Select both → right-click → Merge Columns Change Data Type Wrong type blocking math or chronological sorting Click the type icon on the column header Remove Duplicates Repeated rows quietly inflating totals Right-click column(s) → Remove Duplicates Replace Values Known typos, inconsistent labels Right-click column → Replace Values Trim / Clean Leading/trailing spaces, invisible characters Transform → Format → Trim / Clean Group By Detail rows that need to become one summary row per category Select column(s) → Transform → Group By Merge / Append Queries Two related tables that need to become one Home → Merge Queries / Append Queries Unpivot Columns Wide, one-column-per-period data that charts can't filter by period Select the ID column(s) → right-click the rest → Unpivot Other Columns 25 lessons, real messy data Every card follows the same shape: the before value, why it's a problem, the business impact of leaving it, the exact click-path to fix it, the after value, and what actually changed. Grouped the way you'll meet them in practice — cleaning text first, structure second, values and dates next, then rows, extraction, computed columns, and finally combining whole tables. Never guess a fake number to hide a blank. Either fill it with a defensible business default, or remove the row — and always be ready to explain which choice you made and why. Module 4 · Power Query Editor Next: Dirty → Clean Walkthrough → Cleaning Text Trim & Remove Spaces Customer " Rohit Singh " "Rohit Singh" Leading/trailing spaces are invisible in a cell but not to Power BI — "Rohit Singh" and " Rohit Singh " are two different text values. A "Sales by Customer" chart silently splits one real customer into two shorter bars instead of one tall one. Select the Customer column Transform ribbon → Format → Trim Also run Format → Clean to strip any invisible non-printing characters Leading and trailing whitespace removed; the value now matches every other "Rohit Singh" row exactly. Trim the First Name column in PQ_Practice_Orders.csv — a couple of rows carry visible leading/trailing spaces of their own. Cleaning Text Fix Inconsistent Capitalization Channel "ONLINE", "online", "Online" — three spellings, one channel "Online" Text grouping in Power Query and DAX is case-sensitive — three capitalizations of the same word can be read as three different categories. A bar chart of "Orders by Channel" shows three thin Online bars instead of one tall one, and the real leader isn't obvious anymore. Select the Channel column Transform → Format → lowercase, then Format → Capitalize Each Word Spot-check the result in the column preview before moving on Every spelling variant now renders identically as "Online." Cleaning Text Replace Values Region "Souths" "South" A one-letter typo creates a category that doesn't match anything else in the column. The South region's true total is undercounted by however many rows carry the typo — and a fifth "region" quietly appears in every chart. Right-click the Region column → Replace Values Value To Find: "Souths" · Replace With: "South" The typo'd rows now roll up into the correct region. Cleaning Text Detect Inconsistent Category Values Channel Column looks fine at a glance — until you actually check it A confirmed, short list: Online, Store Casing and typo fixes only work once you know every variant that exists — easy to miss in a column with hundreds of rows. Fixing the 3 variants you noticed while missing a 4th ("Onlin") leaves a silent gap in the cleanup. Click the small chart icon above the column header, or turn on Column Profile in the status bar (bottom-left) Column Distribution shows every distinct value with its count in one glance Cross each variant off a checklist before deciding how to standardize it Nothing yet — this is a detection step, done right before Replace Values / capitalization fixes above. Fixing Structure Rename Columns Quantity Abbreviated headers are fine for the person who exported the file and meaningless to everyone downstream. A teammate building on your query has to guess what "Qty" means instead of reading it. Double-click the column header Type the new name Enter The column header is now self-explanatory — nothing about the data itself changed. Fixing Structure Split a Column Ship City "Bangalore, Karnataka" City = "Bangalore" · State = "Karnataka" City and State are jammed into one text field — you can't filter, slice, or map by State alone while they're combined. A Filled Map by State is impossible until the two values are separated. Select the Ship City column Transform → Split Column → By Delimiter Delimiter: Comma · Split at: Each occurrence of the delimiter Rename the two new columns City and State One combined column becomes two clean, independently filterable columns. Split every row, then build a Filled Map on the new State column. Fixing Structure Merge Columns First Name + Last Name First Name = "Anjali" · Last Name = "Kumar" Full Name = "Anjali Kumar" Two columns that always get used together are more convenient — and often required by a visual — as one. A Table visual meant to show "Customer" cleanly needs one column, not two side by side. Select First Name, then Ctrl-click Last Name Transform → Merge Columns Separator: Space · New column name: Full Name The two source columns are replaced by one combined Full Name column. Fixing Structure Remove Unnecessary Columns Notes A Notes column, blank on every single row Column removed A column with zero populated values carries zero analytical value — it only costs load time and clutters the Fields pane. Every teammate who opens the model has to scroll past a useless field to find the ones that matter. Right-click the Notes column header Remove Columns The model is lighter and the Fields pane only lists columns that actually mean something. Fixing Values Correct Data Types Type shown as ABC123 (Any/Text) — one row contains "N/A" Type: Whole Number A column stuck on a text-like type can't be summed, averaged, or used as a numeric axis, even though most of the values look like numbers. A "Total Units Sold" measure returns blank or an error until the type is fixed. Click the type icon on the Qty column header Choose Whole Number Power Query will flag the "N/A" row as an Error — that's expected, see the next lesson The column is now genuinely numeric, ready for SUM/AVERAGE — except the one row that can't convert. Fixing Values Handle Null/Blank Values Qty (order ORD2006) blank cell row removed (or flagged, not guessed) A blank Qty means you genuinely don't know how many units were ordered — inventing a number would fabricate a sale that may not be real. Silently guessing "1" here means every downstream total includes a number nobody can defend in a review. Right-click Qty → Remove Rows → Remove Blank Rows, if the row truly can't be recovered Or: leave it and flag it for whoever owns the source data, rather than guessing The blank no longer silently pollutes SUM(Qty) — it's either gone or explicitly flagged. Fixing Values Fill Missing Values Discount % (order ORD2017) blank cell Unlike a blank Qty, a blank Discount % has an obvious, defensible default — no value recorded almost always means no discount was applied. Leaving it blank (rather than 0) can break a DIVIDE or make the row silently drop out of a discount-rate average. Right-click Discount % → Replace Values Value To Find: leave blank (null) · Replace With: 0 Every row now has a usable number — filled with a default you can justify out loud, not a guess. Fixing Values Handle Errors Qty (order ORD2011, "N/A") Error (after changing the column to Whole Number) Row removed, or replaced with a justified default An Error value breaks any measure or visual that touches the column until it's dealt with — it doesn't just sit there quietly like a blank does. A published report with unresolved errors shows a red warning icon and can block scheduled refresh entirely. Right-click Qty → Replace Errors (with 0, or a value you can defend) — or — Home → Remove Rows → Remove Errors, if the row should just be excluded Never publish with unresolved errors in a column feeding a measure The column loads clean, with the error either explicitly resolved or the row excluded on purpose. Dates Parse Dates Order Date Type: Text (or a guessed date that's wrong for some rows) Type: Date, verified row by row Power Query guesses a date format from the first few rows and applies it to the whole column — it doesn't check every row. A wrongly-parsed date silently sorts a Line Chart out of chronological order without throwing any error at all. Click the type icon on Order Date Choose Date Scroll through a sample of rows to confirm none of them flipped day/month by mistake The column is genuinely date-typed and ready for a Year/Quarter/Month hierarchy. Dates Handle Inconsistent Date Formats Order Date 03-01-2025, 2025/01/09, 2025-01-15, 25/01/2025 — four formats in one column One consistent format across every row Auto-detected parsing applies ONE format to the whole column and silently mis-reads every row that doesn't match it — 03-01-2025 read as "3rd January" vs "1st March" is a real, undetectable error with no red flag. A monthly trend line can be quietly wrong for months at a time with nothing in the report signaling it. Change the column type to Text first, undoing any auto-date guess Fix the format at the source if possible — or split by format pattern and parse each batch with an explicit Date.FromText format Only change the type to Date once every row uses one confirmed format Every row parses correctly, not just the ones that happened to match the auto-detected pattern. Rows Remove Duplicates entire row (ORD2012 appears twice) Two byte-for-byte identical rows One row An exact duplicate row is the same order counted twice — a data export glitch, not a second sale. Every total the duplicate touches — units, revenue, order count — is inflated by exactly one extra order. Select all columns (Ctrl+A on the column headers) Right-click → Remove Duplicates The order is counted exactly once, matching reality. Rows Filter Rows Status Completed and Cancelled orders mixed together Cancelled rows removed A cancelled order is still a real row in the export, but it never became revenue. Leaving cancelled rows in inflates every sales total by orders that were never actually fulfilled. Click the filter arrow on the Status column header Uncheck "Cancelled" Only orders that actually shipped remain in the table. Rows Sort Data Order Date or Unit Price Rows in export order Rows in a chosen order, for review It's hard to eyeball whether a cleanup step worked when the rows are in arbitrary export order. Not a data-quality issue by itself — it's a working habit that makes every other lesson on this page easier to verify. Click the sort arrow on a column header, or Home → Sort Ascending or Descending Nothing about the data — sorting here is for your own review, and does not control how a Power BI visual sorts later. Extracting Extract Text Product Code "SKU-1001-RED" "RED" The color/variant code is buried inside a compound ID instead of being its own filterable field. You can't build a "Sales by Color" chart until the color exists as its own column. Duplicate the Product Code column first, so the original ID survives Transform → Extract → Text After Delimiter Delimiter: "-" · From: the last occurrence A new column holds just the variant code, ready to use on its own. Extracting Extract Numbers Product Code "SKU-1001-RED" The numeric SKU is mixed with letters, so it can't be sorted or matched numerically as-is. Matching this file to another system's numeric-only SKU list fails until the digits are isolated. On a duplicated copy of Product Code, Transform → Extract → Digits (Or a Custom Column: Text.Select([Product Code], {"0".."9"})) A clean numeric SKU column exists alongside the original compound code. Computed Columns Conditional Columns No size label on an order Order Size = Small / Medium / Large "Qty = 4" doesn't mean anything to a reader scanning a table until it's translated into a business-meaningful bucket. A table sorted or colored by Order Size communicates instantly; one sorted by raw Qty makes the reader do the math themselves. Add Column → Conditional Column Column Name: Order Size If Qty is less than 2 then "Small" · else if Qty is less than or equal to 3 then "Medium" · else "Large" A new, human-readable category column exists without touching the underlying Qty values. Computed Columns Custom Columns Qty × Unit Price Qty and Unit Price as two separate numbers Line Total, one computed column The line-item revenue for an order doesn't exist as a column — it has to be calculated. Without it, every "Total Revenue" visual needs its own DAX measure instead of a simple SUM. Add Column → Custom Column Column Name: Line Total Formula: = [Qty] * [Unit Price] A new column exists that a plain SUM can now total directly. (The one row with Qty = "N/A" will error here too — same fix as the Handle Errors lesson above.) Computed Columns Group Data Category One row per order One row per Category, with totals Sometimes the question is about the category as a whole, not any individual order — that needs summary rows, not detail rows. A quick "how many orders and units per Category" check otherwise means building a whole separate visual just to eyeball it. Select the Category column Transform → Group By New column 1: Order Count · Operation: Count Rows New column 2: Total Qty · Operation: Sum · Column: Qty One summarized table, one row per Category — a separate query from the detail-level Orders table. Combining Data Merge Queries PQ_Practice_Orders.csv + PQ_Practice_Returns.csv Order ID (shared key) Two separate tables, joined by nothing yet Orders with Return Reason and Refund Amount attached where they exist Return information lives in a completely separate export — an order table alone can't show which orders came back. Without merging, "which products get returned most" is impossible to answer from either file alone. Home → Merge Queries First table: Orders · matching column: Order ID Second table: Returns · matching column: Order ID Join Kind: Left Outer (keep every order, attach return info only where it exists) Expand the new column to bring in Return Reason and Refund Amount One combined table — every order, with return details attached for the ones that have them, blank for the ones that don't. Combining Data Append Queries PQ_Practice_Orders.csv + PQ_Practice_Orders_Feb.csv (same columns, different rows) Two monthly export files, same structure One table, both months stacked A new month's export always arrives as its own file with the exact same columns as the last one. Analyzing month-over-month trend is impossible while the months live in two separate tables. Home → Append Queries → Append Queries as New Table 1: the first month's Orders query Table 2: the second month's Orders query One long table, same columns, every row from both months — ready for a real trend line. Combining Data Pivot / Unpivot Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr Region, Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr — one column per month Region, Month, Sales — one row per Region + Month A chart or measure can't filter or slice by "Month" while January, February, March and April are each their own separate column. A Line Chart of Sales trend by Region is impossible to build against the wide layout — Power BI needs Month as values in ONE column, not four column headers. Select the Region column (the one column to KEEP as-is) Right-click → Unpivot Other Columns Rename the two new columns to Month and Sales The same numbers, reshaped from wide to long — now a normal Line Chart or Matrix can use Month as an axis. margin-top:26px card margin-bottom:10px;padding:14px 18px cursor:pointer;font-weight:700;font-family:var(--font-display);font-size:1.05rem;display:flex;justify-content:space-between;gap:10px;align-items:center font-weight:400;font-size:.78rem;color:var(--text-muted);font-family:var(--font-mono) margin-top:14px;padding-top:14px;border-top:1px solid var(--border) grid grid-2 font-size:.85rem font-size:.85rem font-size:.9rem;margin-top:8px s a problem: ${l.issue}
